cards.title: Stopping distance is the total displacement of a vehicle from the instant the…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Stopping distance is the total displacement of a vehicle from the instant the brakes are fully applied until it comes to a complete rest, assuming constant deceleration. It is a scalar quantity measured in metres (m) and depends quadratically on the initial speed and inversely on the magnitude of deceleration.
steps: Imagine you are riding a bicycle at 15 km/h and suddenly apply brakes — you stop within 2-3 metres
Now imagine a car at 60 km/h doing the same
it needs 20+ metres
Why such a huge difference? We begin by recalling the kinematic equation v² = u² + 2as from our study of uniformly accelerated motion
Here final velocity v = 0 (vehicle stops), initial velocity u = v₀, acceleration a is negative (deceleration), and displacement s is the stopping distance
Substitute these into the equation and solve for s
cards.misconception: A wrong answer like ds = v₀/a reveals the student incorrectly used v = u + at instead of v² = u² + 2as, confusing time-based and distance-based kinematic equations.
remember: State the formula for stopping distance of a vehicle in terms of initial velocity v₀ and deceleration a. What are the SI units of each quantity.
A car travelling at 20 m/s stops in 40 m with constant….

cards.title: Reaction time is the time interval between a stimulus (e.g.…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Reaction time is the time interval between a stimulus (e.g., seeing an obstacle) and the initiation of a physical response (e.g., applying brakes), during which the vehicle continues moving at constant initial velocity. Braking distance is the distance traveled from the instant brakes are applied until the vehicle comes to rest under uniform deceleration. The total stopping distance is the sum of reaction distance (v₀ × tᵣ) and braking distance (v₀²/2a), where v₀ is initial velocity (m/s), tᵣ is reaction time (s), and a is magnitude of deceleration (m/s²).
steps: Observe a bicycle rider suddenly spotting a stray dog on a Delhi road — the rider continues moving forward for a fraction of a second before squeezing the brake lever
That "thinking distance" is the reaction distance
In the lab, replicate this by dropping a 30 cm ruler through a classmate's fingers: the distance fallen before catching gives reaction time via d = ½gtᵣ²
Connect this to the kinematic equation v² = u² + 2as used in the previous node (c11_phy_cbse_02_009) for braking distance
The key insight: total stopping distance = v₀tᵣ + v₀²/(2a)
This formula appears in CBSE board exams as both derivation and numerical problems.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., 5 m or 20 m) reveals the student either halves the time incorrectly or confuses reaction distance with braking distance, not recognizing that during reaction time velocity is constant so s = vt applies directly.
remember: A car travels at 20 m/s. The driver's reaction time is 0.5 s. What is the reaction distance traveled before brakes are applied.
Why does the ruler-drop experiment use the formula tᵣ = √(2d/g) instead of tᵣ = d/v? Explain the physical reasoning.
A scooter moving at 15 m/s decelerates at 3 m/s² after a reaction time of 0.6 s. Calculate the total stopping distance.

cards.title: Word problems in motion in a straight line are structured physics questions…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Word problems in motion in a straight line are structured physics questions that describe a real-world kinematic scenario using verbal/textual information, requiring the student to extract given quantities, identify unknowns, select appropriate kinematic equations (v = u + at, s = ut + ½at², v² = u² + 2as), and solve for the required physical quantities with correct SI units and sign conventions. These problems test the ability to translate a physical situation into a mathematical model under the assumption of constant acceleration.
steps: Imagine a motorcycle on the Delhi-Jaipur highway accelerating from a toll plaza: you see the speedometer rise from 0 to 80 km/h in 10 seconds
To solve any word problem, start by visualizing the motion — is the object speeding up, slowing down, or changing direction? Draw a straight line with an arrow showing the chosen positive direction
Mark initial and final positions, velocities, and acceleration vectors
List every number from the text with its unit (convert km/h to m/s!)
Ask: "Which kinematic equation connects my knowns to my unknown?" If time is not given, use v² = u² + 2as
If displacement is not asked, use v = u + at
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., 20 m/s or -20 m/s) reveals the student confuses initial velocity with velocity at the top, or misunderstands that "momentarily at rest" means v = 0 at that instant, not that acceleration is zero (a = -g still acts).

A car moving at 72 km/h applies brakes and stops in 50….
A stone is dropped from a bridge 45 m above a….

cards.title: A scalar is a physical quantity completely specified by its magnitude (a single…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: A scalar is a physical quantity completely specified by its magnitude (a single numerical value with proper SI unit) and has no direction; it obeys ordinary algebraic rules for addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division. A vector is a physical quantity that possesses both magnitude and direction, obeys the triangle law (or equivalently parallelogram law) of vector addition, and is represented by a boldface symbol (e.g., v) or an arrow over a letter (e.g., $\vec{v}$); its magnitude is denoted by $|\vec{v}| = v$.
steps: Observe a ceiling fan in your classroom: the blades rotate at constant speed, so each point on a blade has a speed (scalar) that stays the same, but its velocity (vector) changes continuously because the direction…

Now consider walking from your desk to the blackboard along a curved path — the total distance walked (scalar) depends on the route, but the displacement (vector) is the straight line from start to end, independent of…
Begin by identifying which quantities in your daily life have only magnitude (temperature, mass, time) and which require direction (force, velocity, displacement)
Connect this to Class 9 motion in a straight line where + and – signs handled direction in one dimension, but now in two dimensions we need the full vector language
The key principle: vectors obey the triangle law of addition, which makes them fundamentally different from scalars.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer reveals the student confuses "quantity with units" with "quantity with direction" — e.g., classifying velocity as scalar because it has units m/s, or classifying displacement as scalar because it is measured in metres.

cards.title: The graphical method of vector addition involves representing vectors as…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: The graphical method of vector addition involves representing vectors as directed line segments with lengths proportional to their magnitudes and adding them using the head-to-tail (triangle) method or parallelogram method to obtain a resultant vector whose magnitude and direction represent the combined effect of the individual vectors. The resultant vector R = A + B is found by placing the tail of B at the head of A (triangle method) or by drawing both vectors from a common origin and completing the parallelogram (parallelogram method), with the diagonal representing the resultant. SI unit: same as the vectors being added (e.g., m for displacement, m/s for velocity, N for force).
steps: Watch a boat crossing a river with a steady current: the boat's velocity relative to water and the river's current velocity combine to give the actual path across the river
This is vector addition in real life
Start by drawing the first vector to scale (e.g., 1 cm = 5 m/s) in its given direction using a ruler and protractor
From the head of the first vector, draw the second vector to scale in its direction
The straight line from the tail of the first to the head of the second is the resultant
Measure its length and angle, then convert back using the scale
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., saying they form a parallelogram) reveals confusion between triangle and parallelogram methods, or inability to visualise the head-to-tail arrangement.

cards.title: The analytical method of vector addition resolves each vector into its…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: The analytical method of vector addition resolves each vector into its rectangular components along mutually perpendicular axes (typically x and y), adds the corresponding components algebraically to obtain the resultant's components, and then reconstructs the resultant vector's magnitude and direction using the Pythagorean theorem and trigonometry. This method converts geometric vector addition into algebraic operations on scalar components, enabling precise calculation without scale drawings.
steps: Imagine a kite flying at a 40° angle above the horizontal with a string tension of 15 N
To find how much of this force pulls the kite sideways versus upward, you cannot use a protractor and scale drawing accurately in an exam
Start by drawing a coordinate system with the kite's position as the origin
The horizontal pull is the x-component (15 cos 40°) and the vertical pull is the y-component (15 sin 40°)
This decomposition works because any vector in a plane is the vector sum of two perpendicular components
Connect this to the graphical head-to-tail method you learned: the analytical method simply replaces the geometric construction with trigonometric calculations
cards.misconception: A wrong answer like Fx = 10 N, Fy = 17.3 N reveals the student swapped sine and…
remember: A force vector F has magnitude 20 N and makes an angle of 30° with the positive x-axis. Write its x and y components with correct signs and units.
Why does the component method work for adding vectors that are not perpendicular to each other? Explain using the concept of vector independence along perpendicular directions.
Three forces act on a point: F₁ = 10 N at 0°, F₂ = 15 N at 90°, F₃ = 20 N at 180°. Calculate the magnitude and direction of the resultant force using the component method.

cards.title: Resolution of vectors is the process of splitting a single vector into two or…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Resolution of vectors is the process of splitting a single vector into two or more component vectors along specified directions (usually perpendicular axes) such that their vector sum equals the original vector. In a Cartesian coordinate system, a vector A in the x-y plane is resolved into components Aₓ = A cosθ î and Aᵧ = A sinθ ĵ, where A is the magnitude and θ is the angle with the positive x-axis. The SI unit of each component is the same as the original vector (e.g., m/s for velocity, N for force).
steps: Imagine you are pulling a suitcase with a strap at an angle across a railway platform
Your pull has a forward component that moves the suitcase and an upward component that slightly lifts it off the ground
To analyse this, you must "resolve" your single pull vector into horizontal and vertical parts
Start by drawing the vector as an arrow from the origin
Drop perpendiculars from the tip to the x- and y-axes
the segments on the axes are the components
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., swapping sin/cos or forgetting units) reveals the student does not associate cosine with the adjacent side (x-axis) or sine with the opposite side (y-axis), or they treat components as scalars without unit vectors.
remember: State the x- and y-components of a force vector F = 20 N acting at an angle of 30° with the positive x-axis. Write the vector in unit vector notation.
A velocity vector has components vₓ = -12 m/s and vᵧ = 5….

cards.title: Vector addition using components is the analytical method of finding the…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Vector addition using components is the analytical method of finding the resultant of two or more vectors by resolving each vector into its rectangular components along mutually perpendicular axes (typically x and y), adding the corresponding components algebraically, and then determining the magnitude and direction of the resultant vector from its components. The resultant vector R = A + B has components Rₓ = Aₓ + Bₓ and Rᵧ = Aᵧ + Bᵧ, with magnitude R = √(Rₓ² + Rᵧ²) and direction θ = tan⁻¹(Rᵧ/Rₓ) measured from the +x-axis. SI units for vector components are the same as the vector quantity (e.g., m for displacement, m/s for velocity, N for force).
steps: Imagine a boat crossing a river: the boat's velocity relative to water is 4 m/s at 30° north of east, and the river current flows at 2 m/s due east
To find the boat's actual velocity relative to the ground, you cannot simply add the speeds — you must add the vectors
Start by drawing a coordinate system with +x east and +y north
Resolve each velocity into x and y components using cosine and sine
Add the x-components together and the y-components together
The sums give the resultant's components
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., Fₓ = +5 N) reveals the student does not understand that cosine is negative in the second quadrant (90°–180°) and is likely taking the acute reference angle (60°) without applying the correct sign convention for the quadrant.

cards.title: Multiplication of a vector by a real number (scalar) λ yields a new vector…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Multiplication of a vector by a real number (scalar) λ yields a new vector whose magnitude is |λ| times the magnitude of the original vector, and whose direction is the same as the original vector if λ > 0, opposite if λ < 0, and undefined (null vector) if λ = 0. The operation is denoted as λA and the resultant vector has dimensions equal to the product of the dimensions of λ and A.
steps: Imagine a cyclist riding east at 5 m/s
If she doubles her speed, her velocity vector becomes 10 m/s east – magnitude doubled, direction unchanged
If she reverses direction, her velocity becomes –5 m/s (5 m/s west) – magnitude same, direction opposite
Now ask: what happens if we multiply her velocity vector by the time she rides? The product (velocity × time) gives her displacement vector
Start by identifying the scalar (time) and vector (velocity), then apply the rule: magnitude scales, direction follows the sign of the scalar
This connects directly to the displacement formula s = vt from Class 9 motion.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., magnitude 12 units but direction north) reveals the student thinks a negative scalar only changes magnitude, not direction.

cards.title: The scalar (dot) product of two vectors A and B is a scalar quantity defined as…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: The scalar (dot) product of two vectors A and B is a scalar quantity defined as A·B = |A||B|cosθ, where |A| and |B| are the magnitudes of the vectors and θ is the smaller angle between them when placed tail-to-tail. Its SI unit is the product of the units of the two vectors (e.g., N·m = J for force and displacement). It measures the extent to which one vector projects onto the direction of the other.
steps: Observe a person pushing a heavy box across a floor at an angle: only the component of the push along the floor's direction actually moves the box
This "effective component" is exactly what the dot product captures
Start by recalling vector components from node c11_phy_cbse_03_004: any vector A can be written as Aₓî + Aᵧĵ
The dot product A·B then becomes AₓBₓ + AᵧBᵧ (in 2D) because î·î = 1, ĵ·ĵ = 1, and î·ĵ = 0
This algebraic shortcut avoids measuring angles directly
Connect to the geometric definition: A·B = |A||B|cosθ shows that the dot product is the magnitude of A times the projection of B onto A (or vice versa)
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., giving the cross product formula or forgetting the z-component) reveals the student confuses dot and cross products or treats vectors as purely 2D. Missing the unit indicates they don't track dimensional consistency.

cards.title: The vector (cross) product of two vectors A and B is a vector C = A × B whose…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: The vector (cross) product of two vectors A and B is a vector C = A × B whose magnitude is |A||B| sin θ (where θ is the angle between A and B) and whose direction is perpendicular to the plane containing A and B, given by the right-hand rule. The SI unit of the cross product is the product of the units of the two vectors (e.g., N·m for torque when force in N is crossed with distance in m).
steps: Observe a ceiling fan rotating: the blades push air downward
The rotational effect (torque) depends on the force applied at the blade tip and the distance from the centre, but only the perpendicular component of force matters
This physical situation — where two vectors (position and force) combine to produce a third vector (torque) perpendicular to both — motivates the cross product
Begin by recalling the dot product gives a scalar (work = F·s)
now we need a vector product
Introduce the right-hand rule using a simple hand gesture: curl fingers from first vector to second, thumb gives direction
cards.misconception: A wrong answer of 0 reveals the student thinks parallel vectors have non-zero cross product; an answer with units m reveals confusion with dot product; missing the direction or giving -k̂ shows the right-hand rule is not applied correctly.

cards.title: A position vector r of a particle P in a plane is the vector drawn from a…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: A position vector r of a particle P in a plane is the vector drawn from a chosen origin O to the particle's location, represented as r = xî + yĵ where x, y are Cartesian coordinates (SI unit: metre, m). A displacement vector Δr is the vector from initial position P (at time t) to final position P' (at time t'), given by Δr = r' − r = (x'−x)î + (y'−y)ĵ; its magnitude is the straight-line distance between the two points (SI unit: metre, m) and it is independent of the actual path taken.
steps: Watch a ceiling fan: the tip of a blade moves in a circle
Choose the centre of the fan as origin O
At any instant, the blade tip is at point P
The straight line OP with an arrow from O to P is the position vector — it tells you where the tip is relative to the centre
Now the fan rotates: the tip moves from P to P'
The straight line PP' (arrow from P to P') is the displacement vector — it tells you how the position changed
cards.misconception: A wrong answer like r = 4î + 3ĵ reveals confusion between x and y coordinates. Writing magnitude as 7 m (3+4) shows the student adds components instead of using Pythagoras. Forgetting units (metres) indicates incomplete physical quantity specification.

cards.title: Horizontal projection is a special case of projectile motion where an object is…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Horizontal projection is a special case of projectile motion where an object is launched with an initial velocity that is purely horizontal (projection angle θ₀ = 0°) from a certain height above the ground. The motion is analyzed by treating the horizontal component as uniform motion (aₓ = 0) and the vertical component as free fall under gravity (aᵧ = -g), with the initial vertical velocity component being zero (v₀ᵧ = 0). The path followed is a parabolic trajectory opening downwards.
steps: Observe a cricket ball thrown horizontally from the top of a school building - it moves forward while simultaneously falling downward
Start by setting up a coordinate system: origin at the point of projection, x-axis horizontal along initial velocity, y-axis vertically upward
Recognize that the initial velocity vector has only an x-component (v₀î)
The horizontal motion has zero acceleration, so x = v₀t
The vertical motion is free fall from rest, so y = -½gt²
Eliminate t to get the trajectory equation y = -(g/2v₀²)x²
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., 0 m/s or 20 m/s) reveals the student incorrectly thinks gravity affects horizontal motion or that horizontal velocity changes with time.

cards.title: Projectile motion with angular projection (oblique projection) is the…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Projectile motion with angular projection (oblique projection) is the two-dimensional motion of an object launched with an initial velocity v₀ at an angle θ₀ to the horizontal, moving under the influence of gravity g (9.8 m/s² vertically downward) with negligible air resistance. The motion is analyzed by resolving the initial velocity into horizontal (v₀ cos θ₀) and vertical (v₀ sin θ₀) components, which evolve independently: horizontal motion is uniform (constant velocity), vertical motion is uniformly accelerated (constant acceleration -g).
steps: Imagine a cricket ball bowled at 30 m/s at 40° above horizontal from a height of 2 m
First, observe that the ball follows a curved path - it goes up, slows vertically, stops at the top, then falls down while moving forward steadily
To analyze this, we must separate the motion into two independent one-dimensional motions: horizontal (no force, constant velocity) and vertical (gravity, constant acceleration -g)
Start by drawing a coordinate system: origin at launch point, x horizontal, y vertical upward
Identify given: v₀ = 30 m/s, θ₀ = 40°, g = 9.8 m/s²
The key step is resolving v₀: v₀ₓ = v₀ cos θ₀, v₀ᵧ = v₀ sin θ₀

cards.title: The equation of trajectory of a projectile is the mathematical relationship…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: The equation of trajectory of a projectile is the mathematical relationship between the vertical displacement (y) and horizontal displacement (x) of an object projected with initial velocity \(v_0\) at an angle \(\theta_0\) to the horizontal, under constant gravitational acceleration \(g\) and negligible air resistance. It is given by \(y = x \tan\theta_0 - \frac{g x^2}{2 v_0^2 \cos^2\theta_0}\), which describes a parabolic path in the vertical plane.
steps: Watch a cricket ball hit for a six — it follows a curved path
That curve is not circular
it is a parabola
We already know the horizontal motion is uniform (\(x = v_0 \cos\theta_0 \, t\)) and vertical motion is uniformly accelerated (\(y = v_0 \sin\theta_0 \, t - \frac{1}{2}gt^2\))
To find the shape of the path, we need a direct relation between \(y\) and \(x\) without time
Solve the first equation for \(t = \frac{x}{v_0 \cos\theta_0}\) and substitute into the second
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., missing the \(\cos^2\theta_0\) in the denominator) reveals the student has memorised the formula without understanding the substitution \(t = x/(v_0\cos\theta_0)\).

cards.title: The maximum height (H) of a projectile is the highest vertical position reached…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: The maximum height (H) of a projectile is the highest vertical position reached above the launch point, given by H = (u² sin²θ)/(2g), where u is the initial speed, θ is the projection angle with horizontal, and g is acceleration due to gravity. The horizontal range (R) is the total horizontal distance travelled when the projectile returns to the same vertical level as the launch point, given by R = (u² sin2θ)/g. Both quantities assume no air resistance and a flat horizontal plane.
steps: Observe a cricket ball thrown during a match — it rises to a peak height before falling back to the ground at some distance from the bowler
Notice how the height depends on how steeply it is thrown, and the distance depends on both speed and angle
Start by recalling the vertical motion equations from Class 9 (v = u - gt) and the fact that at maximum height, vertical velocity becomes zero
Use this to find the time to reach the top, then substitute into the vertical displacement equation
For range, use the time of flight (twice the time to max height) multiplied by the constant horizontal velocity

cards.title: Centripetal acceleration is the acceleration experienced by an object moving in…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Centripetal acceleration is the acceleration experienced by an object moving in uniform circular motion, directed radially inward toward the centre of the circle, with magnitude \(a_c = \frac{v^2}{R} = \omega^2 R\), where \(v\) is the constant linear speed (m/s), \(R\) is the radius of the circular path (m), and \(\omega\) is the angular speed (rad/s). It arises solely due to the continuous change in the direction of the velocity vector, while its magnitude remains constant.
steps: Observe a ceiling fan running at constant speed: the blades move in a circle, yet they are accelerating because their velocity direction changes at every instant
To begin, draw the circular path and mark two nearby positions P and P′
Draw velocity vectors \(\vec{v}\) and \(\vec{v}'\) tangent to the circle at those points
Using the triangle law of vector addition, find \(\Delta \vec{v} = \vec{v}' - \vec{v}\)
Notice that \(\Delta \vec{v}\) points toward the centre
As \(\Delta t \to 0\), the average acceleration \(\Delta \vec{v}/\Delta t\) becomes the instantaneous centripetal acceleration \(\vec{a}_c\), always directed radially inward
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., \(a_c = vR\) or unit m/s) reveals confusion between acceleration and velocity, or failure to square the speed.

cards.title: Aristotle's fallacy is the incorrect assertion that a continuous external force…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Aristotle's fallacy is the incorrect assertion that a continuous external force is required to maintain a body in uniform motion; Galileo's experiments with inclined planes demonstrated that in the absence of friction, a body in uniform motion continues indefinitely without any external force, establishing the law of inertia: a body remains in its state of rest or uniform motion in a straight line unless compelled by a net external force to change that state.
steps: Observe a marble rolling on a smooth floor versus a rough carpet—on the smooth floor it travels farther before stopping
Now imagine a perfectly frictionless horizontal surface (like an air hockey table with the air on): the marble would never stop
This thought experiment mirrors Galileo's insight: he asked what happens to a ball rolling down one smooth incline and up another
as the second incline flattens to horizontal, the ball rolls farther to reach the same height, implying infinite distance on a frictionless horizontal plane

Start by identifying the hidden force (friction) in everyday experience, then trace Galileo's logical extrapolation to the idealised frictionless case, and conclude with the law of inertia as the correct principle.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., "gravity stops the motion") reveals confusion between the vertical force of gravity and the horizontal retarding force of friction.

cards.title: Newton's First Law of Motion (Law of Inertia) states that a body remains in its…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Newton's First Law of Motion (Law of Inertia) states that a body remains in its state of rest or uniform motion in a straight line unless acted upon by a net external force; equivalently, if the net external force on a body is zero, its acceleration is zero. Inertia is the intrinsic property of matter that quantifies resistance to change in motion, measured by mass (SI unit: kg).
steps: Observe a book resting on your classroom desk — it stays at rest until you push it
Now imagine a hockey puck sliding on perfectly smooth ice: it continues with nearly constant velocity for a long distance
These everyday observations reveal that a net external force is needed to change motion, not to sustain it

Since the book is at rest, the First Law tells us net force is zero, so R = mg

cards.title: Newton's Second Law states that the rate of change of linear momentum of a body…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Newton's Second Law states that the rate of change of linear momentum of a body is directly proportional to the net external force acting on it and occurs in the direction of that force. For a body of constant mass m, this reduces to F = ma, where F is the net external force (SI unit: newton, N = kg·m·s⁻²), m is the mass (kg), and a is the acceleration (m·s⁻²). The law is a vector equation valid in an inertial frame.
steps: Watch a cricket fielder catching a fast ball — they pull their hands backward, increasing the stopping time
Why? The ball's momentum changes from mv to zero
If caught with rigid hands, Δt is tiny, so F = Δp/Δt is huge and hurts
By increasing Δt, the fielder reduces the force
This is Newton's Second Law in action: force depends on how fast momentum changes

cards.title: Newton's Third Law states that for every force exerted by body A on body B…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Newton's Third Law states that for every force exerted by body A on body B, there exists a simultaneous force of equal magnitude but opposite direction exerted by body B on body A. These paired forces are called action and reaction, and they always act on different bodies. The law is expressed mathematically as F_AB = –F_BA, where F_AB is the force on A by B and F_BA is the force on B by A, both measured in newtons (N). This law applies universally to all force types (gravitational, electromagnetic, contact) and is the foundation for momentum conservation in isolated systems.
steps: Place a heavy book on a spring balance held vertically
Observe the reading
Now pull the spring balance downward with your hand while the book rests on it — the reading increases
Ask: "Which force is action, which is reaction?" The book pushes down on the spring (action), the spring pushes up on the book (reaction)
But your hand pulls the spring down — the spring pulls your hand up
This chain of pairs reveals that forces never exist alone

cards.title: Momentum (p) of a body is the product of its mass (m) and velocity (v)…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Momentum (p) of a body is the product of its mass (m) and velocity (v), expressed as p = mv. It is a vector quantity with SI unit kg·m/s, measuring the quantity of motion and the resistance to change in motion. Impulse (I) is the product of net force (F) and the time interval (Δt) over which it acts, equal to the change in momentum: I = FΔt = Δp, with SI unit N·s (equivalent to kg·m/s).
steps: Watch a cricket match: when a fielder catches a fast ball, they pull their hands backward, increasing the stopping time
If they kept hands rigid, the ball stops in milliseconds, exerting huge force that hurts
This everyday observation reveals that force depends not just on momentum change but on how quickly it occurs
We start by defining momentum p = mv from Class 9, then use Newton's second law F = ma = m(dv/dt) = d(mv)/t = dp/dt to show force equals rate of momentum change
Integrating over time gives impulse I = ∫F dt = Δp
The key insight: a small force acting long can produce the same momentum change as a large force acting briefly.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., giving impulse as N or J) reveals confusion between impulse (force × time) and work/energy (force × distance), or failure to recognize that N·s simplifies to kg·m/s.

cards.title: The law of conservation of momentum states that for an isolated system (no net…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: The law of conservation of momentum states that for an isolated system (no net external force), the total vector momentum remains constant in time: \(\sum \vec{p}_{\text{initial}} = \sum \vec{p}_{\text{final}}\). Momentum \(\vec{p} = m\vec{v}\) is a vector quantity measured in kg·m/s. The law follows directly from Newton's second and third laws and holds for all collisions and explosions in isolated systems, regardless of whether kinetic energy is conserved.
steps: Watch a cricket bowler deliver a ball: the ball gains forward momentum while the bowler experiences a tiny backward recoil
Now imagine the same interaction on a frictionless icy lake — the total momentum of bowler+ball system before release (zero) equals total momentum after

Begin by identifying the system boundaries: are external forces (friction, gravity component along motion) negligible during the brief interaction? If yes, apply \(\sum \vec{p}_i = \sum \vec{p}_f\) as a vector equation
Break into x and y components
For 1D problems, choose a sign convention
Always verify isolation assumption before writing the conservation equation.

cards.title: Equilibrium of a particle is the state in which the vector sum of all external…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Equilibrium of a particle is the state in which the vector sum of all external forces acting on the particle is zero (ΣF = 0), resulting in zero acceleration. The particle either remains at rest or moves with constant velocity in a straight line. For concurrent forces, equilibrium requires that the forces can be represented by the sides of a closed polygon taken in the same cyclic order, or equivalently, that the algebraic sum of force components along any two perpendicular axes is zero (ΣFₓ = 0, ΣFᵧ = 0).
steps: Observe a ceiling fan hanging from a hook by a rod — it remains stationary despite gravity pulling it down
The hook exerts an upward force exactly balancing the weight
Now imagine pushing a book on a table horizontally with 5 N while friction pushes back with 5 N — the book stays at rest
In both cases, forces cancel out vectorially

cards.title: Common forces in mechanics are the fundamental contact and non-contact forces…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Common forces in mechanics are the fundamental contact and non-contact forces encountered in classical mechanics problems: gravitational force (weight, W = mg, acting vertically downward), normal reaction (N, perpendicular to contact surfaces), friction (static fs ≤ μsN opposing impending motion, kinetic fk = μkN opposing relative motion), tension (T, along a massless inextensible string), and spring force (F = -kx, restoring force proportional to displacement). These forces originate macroscopically from electromagnetic interactions between charged constituents of matter, except gravity which is a fundamental force.
steps: Observe a book resting on your study table
It experiences gravity pulling down, yet it doesn't fall through the table
The table must push up with a normal force
Now push the book gently horizontally - it doesn't move until your push exceeds a limit
That limiting force is static friction
Once moving, a smaller kinetic friction opposes motion

cards.title: Friction is a contact force that opposes the relative motion or tendency of…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Friction is a contact force that opposes the relative motion or tendency of relative motion between two surfaces in contact. Static friction (f_s) acts when surfaces are at rest relative to each other, varying from zero up to a maximum value f_s(max) = μ_s N. Kinetic friction (f_k) acts when surfaces slide relative to each other, with magnitude f_k = μ_k N, where μ_k < μ_s. The SI unit of friction is newton (N), and coefficients of friction (μ_s, μ_k) are dimensionless constants depending only on the nature of the surfaces in contact.
steps: Observe a heavy wooden cupboard in your classroom - you push it gently and it doesn't move
push harder and it suddenly starts sliding, but once moving, you need less force to keep it moving at constant speed
This everyday experience reveals two distinct friction behaviors
Begin by identifying the two contact surfaces and drawing the free-body diagram showing weight (mg), normal reaction (N), applied force (F), and friction (f)
The key is recognizing that static friction is self-adjusting (f_s ≤ μ_s N) while kinetic friction is constant (f_k = μ_k N)
Connect this to Newton's first law (equilibrium when net force is zero) and second law (acceleration when net force is non-zero)
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., 0.8 N or 80 N) reveals the student either forgot to multiply by g (confusing mass with weight) or misplaced the decimal point, indicating poor unit tracking or confusion between mass and weight.

cards.title: The coefficient of friction (μ) is a dimensionless scalar quantity that…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: The coefficient of friction (μ) is a dimensionless scalar quantity that represents the ratio of the frictional force (f) between two surfaces to the normal reaction force (N) pressing them together. For static friction, μ_s = f_s_max / N where f_s_max is the maximum static friction before motion begins; for kinetic friction, μ_k = f_k / N where f_k is the constant friction during relative motion. Both coefficients depend only on the nature of the two surfaces in contact.
steps: Observe a heavy wooden box on a classroom floor: it doesn't move when you push gently, but starts sliding when you push hard enough
Notice that once moving, you need less force to keep it moving at constant speed than to start it
This reveals two distinct friction regimes
Begin by drawing a free-body diagram of the box at rest, identifying the normal force N = mg
The maximum static friction f_s_max = μ_s N is the threshold
if applied force F ≤ f_s_max, the box stays at rest with f_s = F
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., giving units of N or writing f_s = μ_s N always) reveals the student thinks μ_s has units or that static friction always takes its maximum value, ignoring its self-adjusting nature.

cards.title: Rolling friction is the resistive force that opposes the motion of a body (such…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Rolling friction is the resistive force that opposes the motion of a body (such as a wheel, sphere, or cylinder) rolling without slipping over a surface. It arises due to local deformation of the rolling body and/or the surface at the contact region, creating a finite contact area whose resultant reaction force has a component opposite to the direction of motion. Its magnitude is typically 2–3 orders of magnitude smaller than static or kinetic friction for the same normal load. Lubrication is the process of introducing a fluid (liquid or gas) between two solid surfaces in relative motion to replace solid–solid contact with fluid film shear, thereby drastically reducing the coefficient of friction and wear.
steps: Observe a steel ball bearing rolling on a glass table versus sliding a steel block on the same table — the ball rolls much farther with the same initial push
This shows rolling friction is far smaller
Begin by recalling static and kinetic friction from c11_phy_cbse_04_009 and c11_phy_cbse_04_010: they oppose relative motion between surfaces in contact

Now ask: what happens when a wheel rolls without slipping? The contact point is instantaneously at rest relative to the ground, so static friction could act, but in ideal rigid bodies there would be zero resistance
Real surfaces deform, creating a small contact patch
The normal reaction shifts forward, producing a torque that opposes rolling
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., "rolling friction is larger than static friction") reveals the student confuses the ease of rolling with the magnitude of the resistive force, or thinks friction always increases with contact area.
remember: Define rolling friction and state how its magnitude compares to static and kinetic friction for the same normal force.

cards.title: Centripetal force is the net force directed toward the center of a circular…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Centripetal force is the net force directed toward the center of a circular path that causes a particle to follow that curved trajectory, with magnitude given by \(F_c = \frac{m v^2}{R} = m \omega^2 R\) where \(m\) is the mass of the particle, \(v\) its linear speed, \(\omega\) its angular speed, and \(R\) the radius of the circle. It is not a new kind of force but the radial component of the net force arising from physical interactions like tension, friction, gravity, or normal reaction.
steps: Watch a ceiling fan starting from rest: the blades accelerate until they reach a constant speed, yet each blade tip continuously changes direction
Ask: what force keeps the tip moving in a circle? The answer lies in the internal stresses of the blade material providing the inward pull
Next, consider a bicycle turning on a level road: the rider leans inward, and the friction between tyres and road supplies the necessary centripetal force
Connect this to Newton's second law: the net force toward the centre equals mass times centripetal acceleration (\(v^2/R\))
Finally, introduce the formula \(F_c = m v^2/R\) and emphasize that the specific force (friction, tension, normal component) depends on the physical situation.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer like \(F_c = m v R\) or missing the square on \(v\) reveals confusion between centripetal force and momentum or a misunderstanding of the acceleration formula \(a_c = v^2/R\).
remember: State the formula for centripetal force in terms of mass \(m\), linear speed \(v\), and radius \(R\). Give its SI unit.

A cyclist leans at an angle of 30° to the vertical while negotiating a circular bend of radius 10 m on a level….

cards.title: Banking of roads is the practice of raising the outer edge of a curved road…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Banking of roads is the practice of raising the outer edge of a curved road above the inner edge at an angle θ (angle of banking) so that the horizontal component of the normal reaction provides the necessary centripetal force for a vehicle to negotiate the curve safely, reducing or eliminating dependence on friction. The optimum speed v₀ = √(Rg tan θ) is the speed at which no friction is required, while the maximum permissible speed v_max = √[Rg (tan θ + μ_s)/(1 - μ_s tan θ)] is the highest speed without skidding, where R is the radius of curvature, g = 9.8 m/s², and μ_s is the coefficient of static friction.
steps: Observe a highway flyover curve near your city — the outer edge is visibly higher than the inner edge
Place a coin on a tilted book and spin it: at a certain tilt, the coin goes in a circle without sliding
This is banking in action
Begin by drawing a free-body diagram of a car on a banked road: weight mg down, normal reaction N perpendicular to surface, friction f parallel to surface
Resolve N and f into vertical and horizontal components
Apply equilibrium in vertical direction (N cos θ = mg + f sin θ) and centripetal force requirement horizontally (N sin θ + f cos θ = mv²/R)
cards.misconception: A wrong answer using v = √(Rg sin θ) or v = √(Rg) reveals the student cannot distinguish between the components of normal reaction and incorrectly assumes the full normal force provides centripetal force, or confuses banking with level road formula v_max =…

A banked curve has radius 300 m and banking angle 15°. The coefficient of static friction is 0.2. Calculate the maximum permissible speed in km/h. Take g = 9.8 m/s².

cards.title: A Free Body Diagram (FBD) is a schematic representation of an isolated body (or…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: A Free Body Diagram (FBD) is a schematic representation of an isolated body (or system) showing all external forces acting on it, with each force drawn as a vector originating from the body's center of mass, labeled by its type (e.g., weight, normal reaction, tension, friction) and magnitude. It is the primary tool for applying Newton's Second Law (ΣF = ma) in component form to solve mechanics problems involving equilibrium or accelerated motion.
steps: Imagine a loaded rickshaw parked on a sloped street in Shimla — the driver applies the handbrake, yet you notice the rear wheels are turned slightly toward the curb
Why? To solve this, first observe the real situation: identify the rickshaw as the "system," isolate it mentally from the road, gravity, and brake cable

Next, list every push/pull acting on it: weight (mg) vertically down, normal reaction (N) perpendicular to slope, static friction (fs) parallel to slope opposing impending motion, and brake cable tension (T) at the…
Draw the FBD as a dot with four labeled arrows
Then choose axes — one parallel to the slope (x), one perpendicular (y) — because acceleration is constrained along the slope
Finally, apply ΣFx = max and ΣFy = 0 (no vertical acceleration) to find the minimum friction coefficient needed
cards.misconception: A wrong answer reveals the student memorizes "draw arrows" but lacks the systematic algorithm to handle multi-body systems — they will miss forces or misapply Third Law when connecting subsystems.
remember: State the five sequential steps of the standard Free Body Diagram procedure for solving a mechanics problem, as prescribed in the NCERT Class 11 textbook (Section 4.11).

cards.title: Work done by a constant force is defined as the scalar product of the force…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Work done by a constant force is defined as the scalar product of the force vector and the displacement vector of the point of application of the force. Mathematically, \( W = \vec{F} \cdot \vec{d} = F d \cos\theta \), where \( F \) is the magnitude of the force, \( d \) is the magnitude of the displacement, and \( \theta \) is the angle between the force and displacement vectors. Work is a scalar quantity measured in joules (J), where 1 J = 1 N·m. Work is done only when the force has a component along the direction of displacement.
steps: Observe a coolie carrying a heavy suitcase on his head while walking horizontally on a railway platform — he sweats and gets tired, yet in physics the work done by his upward force on the suitcase is zero
This surprises students because the force (upward) and displacement (horizontal) are perpendicular
Start by asking: "What must be measured to decide if work is done?" Guide them to recognise that both force and displacement are vectors, and only the component of force along displacement matters
Introduce the dot product as the mathematical tool that extracts this component

Conclude with the formula \( W = F d \cos\theta \) and emphasise that \( \cos\theta \) determines the sign: positive for \( \theta < 90^\circ \), negative for \( \theta > 90^\circ \), zero for \( \theta = 90^\circ \).
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., calculating \( mgh \) or \( F \times d \)) reveals the student is using the everyday meaning of "work" (effort) instead of the physics definition, or they incorrectly assume force and displacement are parallel.

cards.title: Work done by a variable force is the definite integral of the force component…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Work done by a variable force is the definite integral of the force component along the displacement over the path of motion: \( W = \int_{x_i}^{x_f} F(x) \, dx \), where \( F(x) \) is the magnitude of the force component in the direction of displacement as a function of position \( x \). Its SI unit is joule (J), equivalent to newton-metre (N·m). This calculates the total energy transferred when force magnitude or direction changes continuously during displacement.
steps: Observe a spring balance being stretched slowly: the force you apply increases steadily from zero to a maximum value
Unlike pushing a box with constant force, here the force changes with displacement
To find total work, we cannot simply multiply final force by distance
Instead, break the stretch into tiny steps \( \Delta x \) where force is nearly constant, compute \( F(x) \Delta x \) for each step, and sum them
As \( \Delta x \to 0 \), this sum becomes the integral \( \int F(x) \, dx \)
This connects directly to the Class 9 concept of work as area under a force-displacement graph (rectangle for constant force, now a curve for variable force)
cards.misconception: A wrong answer like \( W = F \cdot \Delta x \) (using only final force) reveals the student still treats variable force as constant. Writing unit as newton (N) instead of joule shows confusion between force and work dimensions.

cards.title: The work done by a spring force is the negative of the change in elastic…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: The work done by a spring force is the negative of the change in elastic potential energy stored in the spring, calculated as the integral of the variable restoring force \(F_s = -kx\) over the displacement from initial position \(x_i\) to final position \(x_f\). It is a scalar quantity measured in joules (J), given by \(W_s = \frac{1}{2}k(x_i^2 - x_f^2)\), where \(k\) is the spring constant (N/m) and \(x\) is displacement from the equilibrium position. The negative sign indicates the spring force always opposes the displacement, doing negative work when the spring is stretched or compressed from equilibrium, and positive work when returning toward equilibrium.
steps: Observe a common door closer or a spring-loaded pen in your classroom — when you push the door or click the pen, you feel a resisting force that increases the more you compress the spring
This is Hooke's law in action: the spring force is not constant but grows linearly with displacement
To find the work done by this variable force, we cannot use \(W = Fd\) directly
we must integrate
Start by drawing the \(F\) vs \(x\) graph — a straight line through origin with slope \(-k\)
The work done is the signed area under this line between \(x_i\) and \(x_f\), forming a trapezoid (or triangle if starting from equilibrium)
cards.misconception: A wrong answer like \(W_s = \frac{1}{2}k(x_f^2 - x_i^2)\) reveals the student has confused the work done BY the spring with the work done ON the spring (or the potential energy change), missing the crucial negative sign convention.
remember: State the formula for work done by a spring force when a block attached to a spring moves from displacement \(x_i\) to \(x_f\). Define each symbol and its SI unit.

cards.title: Kinetic energy is the energy possessed by a body due to its motion…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Kinetic energy is the energy possessed by a body due to its motion, defined as the work needed to accelerate a body of mass \( m \) from rest to velocity \( \vec{v} \). For a particle of mass \( m \) moving with speed \( v \), its kinetic energy \( K \) is given by \( K = \frac{1}{2} m v^2 \). It is a scalar quantity, always non-negative, with SI unit joule (J) and dimensions \([ML^2T^{-2}]\).
steps: Observe a cricket ball and a tennis ball thrown at the same speed — the cricket ball hurts more because it has more mass
Now imagine the same cricket ball thrown at different speeds — the faster one does more damage
This shows kinetic energy depends on both mass and speed
In Class 9 you learned \( v^2 - u^2 = 2as \) and multiplied by \( m/2 \) to get \( \frac{1}{2}mv^2 - \frac{1}{2}mu^2 = mas = Fs = W \)
The quantity \( \frac{1}{2}mv^2 \) is kinetic energy, and the change in it equals the net work done
Start by measuring mass (kg) and speed (m/s), then apply \( K = \frac{1}{2}mv^2 \).

cards.title: The work-energy theorem states that the net work done by all forces acting on a…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: The work-energy theorem states that the net work done by all forces acting on a particle equals the change in its kinetic energy: \(W_{\text{net}} = \Delta K = K_f - K_i = \frac{1}{2}mv_f^2 - \frac{1}{2}mv_i^2\). The SI unit of work and kinetic energy is the joule (J), where 1 J = 1 N·m = 1 kg·m²/s².
steps: Imagine a bicycle moving on a level road: when you pedal, you do positive work and the bicycle speeds up
when you apply brakes, friction does negative work and the bicycle slows down
This everyday observation connects force, displacement, and speed change
To quantify it, we start with the familiar kinematic equation \(v^2 - u^2 = 2as\) from Class 9
Multiply both sides by \(m/2\) and substitute \(ma = F_{\text{net}}\) (Newton's second law)
The left side becomes the difference in \(\frac{1}{2}mv^2\), which we define as kinetic energy
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., stating \(W = mv\) or omitting the 1/2 factor) reveals confusion between momentum and kinetic energy or a missing factor from the derivation.
remember: State the work-energy theorem in words and give its mathematical expression for a particle of mass \(m\) whose velocity changes from \(v_i\) to….

cards.title: The work-energy theorem for a variable force states that the change in kinetic…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: The work-energy theorem for a variable force states that the change in kinetic energy of a particle equals the net work done by the resultant variable force acting on it as it moves from an initial position to a final position. Mathematically, \(K_f - K_i = W_{\text{net}} = \int_{x_i}^{x_f} F_{\text{net}}(x) \, dx\), where \(K = \frac{1}{2}mv^2\) is kinetic energy in joules (J), \(F_{\text{net}}(x)\) is the net force as a function of displacement in newtons (N), and the integral represents the area under the force-displacement graph.
steps: Watch a spring-loaded toy car released from a compressed spring on a smooth floor: the spring force decreases linearly as the spring expands, so the force is not constant
To find the car's speed when the spring reaches natural length, you cannot use \(W = Fd\) because \(F\) changes

Instead, you break the motion into tiny displacements \(\Delta x\) where force is nearly constant, sum the work pieces \(\sum F(x)\Delta x\), and take the limit as \(\Delta x \to 0\) to get the integral \(\int F(x)dx\)
This integral equals the change in kinetic energy \(\frac{1}{2}mv_f^2 - \frac{1}{2}mv_i^2\)
Start by drawing the force-displacement graph, identify the function \(F(x)\), set up the integral with correct limits, and equate to \(\Delta K\).
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., writing \(W = F\Delta x\) or omitting the integral) reveals the student still thinks work is only force times distance and has not internalized the limiting process for variable forces.
remember: State the work-energy theorem for a variable force in one dimension, defining all symbols and giving the SI unit of each term.

cards.title: Gravitational potential energy near Earth's surface is the energy stored in a…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Gravitational potential energy near Earth's surface is the energy stored in a body-Earth system due to the body's position (height) relative to a chosen reference level. It is defined as V(h) = mgh, where m is mass (kg), g is acceleration due to gravity (9.8 m/s²), and h is vertical height above the reference level (m). The SI unit is joule (J). This formula assumes g is constant (h << Earth's radius) and the zero of potential energy is arbitrarily chosen (usually ground level).
steps: Observe a water tank on a rooftop in an Indian household
Water flows down through pipes due to gravity — the energy to move water comes from its height

Start by asking: "If you lift a 2 kg bucket of water from ground to a 10 m high terrace, how much energy is stored?" Connect to prior concept: work done against gravity (W = mgh) from Class 9 (c9_physics_ch4_6)
The work done by the external force gets stored as potential energy
The key formula is V(h) = mgh, but emphasize that only ΔV = mgΔh is physically meaningful because the zero reference is arbitrary.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer like 112.7 J (using final height only) reveals the student thinks V(h) = mgh gives absolute energy rather than understanding only ΔV is…
remember: A 5 kg object is raised from a table (height 0.8 m) to a shelf (height 2.3 m). What is the change in its gravitational potential energy? (Take g = 9.8 m/s²).

cards.title: The elastic potential energy of a spring is the energy stored in a spring due…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: The elastic potential energy of a spring is the energy stored in a spring due to its deformation (extension or compression) from its equilibrium position, given by the formula $U = \frac{1}{2}kx^2$ where $k$ is the spring constant (SI unit: N/m) and $x$ is the displacement from equilibrium (SI unit: m). It is a scalar quantity measured in joules (J) and represents the work done by an external agent against the conservative spring force $F_s = -kx$ to stretch or compress the spring, assuming the spring obeys Hooke's law and is massless.
steps: Observe a common spring balance used in Indian vegetable markets — when you hang a 1 kg tomato bag, the spring stretches by about 5 cm
This visible stretch stores energy that would launch the tomatoes upward if released suddenly
Begin by measuring the spring constant $k$ using Hooke's law: hang known masses, measure extension $x$, plot $F$ vs $x$, the slope gives $k$
Connect this to the previous node on gravitational potential energy — just as $mgh$ stores energy by height, $\frac{1}{2}kx^2$ stores energy by configuration
The key formula emerges from integrating the variable spring force: $W = \int F\,dx = \int -kx\,dx = -\frac{1}{2}kx^2$, so the stored potential energy is the negative of this work.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., writing $U = kx$ or giving $k$ in N) reveals confusion between force and energy, or misunderstanding that $k$ is a property of the spring, not the deformation.
remember: State the formula for elastic potential energy of a spring and write the SI units of each variable. What is the physical significance of the spring constant $k$.

cards.title: A force is conservative if the work done by it on an object moving between two…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: A force is conservative if the work done by it on an object moving between two points depends only on the initial and final positions, not on the path taken; equivalently, the work done by a conservative force over any closed loop is zero. A force is non-conservative if the work done depends on the path taken, so the work over a closed loop is non-zero (typically negative for dissipative forces like friction). The SI unit of work (and energy) is the joule (J). Conservative forces allow the definition of a potential energy function \( V(\vec{r}) \) such that \( \vec{F} = -\nabla V \); non-conservative forces do not have an associated potential energy.
steps: Observe a block sliding down two different ramps of the same height from rest: one smooth, one rough
On the smooth ramp, the block reaches the bottom with the same speed regardless of the ramp's shape (straight, curved, stepped) – only the vertical height matters
On the rough ramp, the final speed depends on the ramp's length and shape because friction does more work over a longer path
This path-dependence is the hallmark of a non-conservative force
Begin by asking: "If I move a book from the floor to a table via a straight lift versus a long winding path, does gravity do the same…
The key principle: For a conservative force, \( W_{\text{closed}} = 0 \) and \( \vec{F} = -\nabla V \)
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., "work depends on path" or "unit is newton") reveals the student confuses conservative with non-conservative forces or confuses force and work units.
remember: State the defining property of a conservative force in terms of work done over a closed path. What is the SI unit of work.

cards.title: The principle of conservation of mechanical energy states that in an isolated…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: The principle of conservation of mechanical energy states that in an isolated system where only conservative forces (e.g., gravitational force, spring force) do work, the total mechanical energy — defined as the sum of kinetic energy (K = ½mv²) and potential energy (V) — remains constant throughout the motion: E = K + V = constant. This means ΔK + ΔV = 0, or equivalently, Ki + Vi = Kf + Vf, where i and f denote initial and final states. The SI unit of mechanical energy is joule (J).
steps: Observe a simple pendulum in your school lab — pull the bob to one side and release it
Notice how it swings back and forth, rising to nearly the same height on each side
At the highest points, the bob momentarily stops (K = 0) and has maximum gravitational potential energy (V = mgh)
At the lowest point, it moves fastest (maximum K) and has minimum V (zero if we choose the reference there)
The sum K + V stays constant if air resistance is negligible
This is the essence of conservation of mechanical energy
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., stating "energy is always conserved" without the conservative force condition, or confusing mechanical energy with total energy) reveals the student has memorized the formula without understanding the crucial condition — that…

cards.title: Power is the rate at which work is done or energy is transferred.
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Power is the rate at which work is done or energy is transferred. It is a scalar quantity defined as the time derivative of work: P = dW/dt. The SI unit is the watt (W), where 1 W = 1 J/s. For a constant force, instantaneous power can also be expressed as P = F·v, where F is the force and v is the instantaneous velocity of the point of application.
steps: Observe a ceiling fan in your classroom: it does work on the air by pushing it downwards, but what makes one fan "more powerful" than another? It is not just the total work done, but how fast it does that work
Start by measuring the work done by the fan in 10 seconds (using force and displacement of air) and then divide by time to get average power
Connect this to the prior concept of work (c11_phy_cbse_05_001) — power is simply work per unit time
Then consider a cyclist accelerating: the force and velocity change instantaneously, so we need instantaneous power P = F·v
The key formula is P_avg = W/t and P_inst = dW/dt = F·v.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., saying unit is joule) reveals confusion between work/energy and power — the student has not grasped that power is a rate, not an amount.
remember: State the SI unit of power and write its dimensional formula. How is it related to the units of work and time.

cards.title: Average power is the total work done divided by the total time interval over…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Average power is the total work done divided by the total time interval over which the work is performed, while instantaneous power is the limiting value of average power as the time interval approaches zero, equal to the dot product of the net force acting on a body and its instantaneous velocity (P = F·v). Both are scalar quantities measured in watts (W), where 1 W = 1 J/s.
steps: Observe a ceiling fan starting from rest: initially it takes large force to overcome inertia, but once at constant speed, the motor only balances friction
The power needed at startup (instantaneous) is much higher than the average power over the first minute
Begin by recalling the definition of work (W = F·d) and average power (P_avg = W/t)
Ask: "What if the force or velocity changes during the motion?" Introduce the limit Δt → 0 to define instantaneous power
Show that dW = F·dr leads to P = F·v
Emphasize that this is a scalar product, so only the component of force along velocity matters
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., giving unit as joule or newton) reveals confusion between work and power, or missing the time aspect of power.
remember: State the SI unit of power and write the formula for average power in terms of work and time.

cards.title: A collision is an isolated event where two or more bodies exert strong…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: A collision is an isolated event where two or more bodies exert strong impulsive forces on each other for a very short time interval Δt, resulting in a change in their momenta. In an elastic collision, the total kinetic energy of the system is conserved (Kᵢ = K_f) along with total linear momentum. In an inelastic collision, total linear momentum is conserved but total kinetic energy is not conserved (K_f < Kᵢ); a completely inelastic collision is the extreme case where the bodies stick together and move with a common final velocity. The coefficient of restitution e = (v₂f - v₁f)/(v₁i - v₂i) quantifies elasticity (e = 1 for elastic, e = 0 for completely inelastic, 0 < e < 1 for inelastic).

cards.title: A one-dimensional collision is an interaction between two bodies where their…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: A one-dimensional collision is an interaction between two bodies where their initial and final velocities are directed along the same straight line, and momentum is conserved while kinetic energy may or may not be conserved depending on whether the collision is perfectly elastic or inelastic. The SI unit for momentum is kg·m/s and for kinetic energy is joule (J).

When they collide head-on, they move along the same line
Start by identifying the system: two masses m1 and m2 with initial velocities u1 and u2
Apply momentum conservation: m1u1 + m2u2 = m1v1 + m2v2
For elastic collisions, add kinetic energy conservation: ½m1u1² + ½m2u2² = ½m1v1² + ½m2v2²

cards.title: A collision in two dimensions occurs when two bodies interact such that their…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: A collision in two dimensions occurs when two bodies interact such that their initial and final velocities lie in a plane, requiring vector momentum conservation in two perpendicular directions (typically x and y axes). For an isolated system, the total linear momentum vector is conserved: \( m_1\vec{v}_{1i} + m_2\vec{v}_{2i} = m_1\vec{v}_{1f} + m_2\vec{v}_{2f} \), yielding two independent scalar component equations. In elastic collisions, kinetic energy is also conserved: \( \frac{1}{2}m_1v_{1i}^2 + \frac{1}{2}m_2v_{2i}^2 = \frac{1}{2}m_1v_{1f}^2 + \frac{1}{2}m_2v_{2f}^2 \). The SI unit for momentum is kg·m/s and for energy is joule (J).

This everyday observation reveals that momentum, being a vector, must be conserved separately along the x-direction (initial motion) and y-direction (perpendicular)

This mirrors the standard board exam pattern where \( \theta_2 \) (pocket angle) is given and \( \theta_1 \) is asked.

cards.title: The centre of mass of a system of particles is the unique point where the…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: The centre of mass of a system of particles is the unique point where the entire mass of the system can be considered to be concentrated for the purpose of analyzing its translational motion under external forces. It is defined by the position vector R = (1/M) Σ m_i r_i for discrete particles, or R = (1/M) ∫ r dm for a continuous mass distribution, where M = Σ m_i is the total mass, m_i is the mass of the i-th particle, and r_i is its position vector from a chosen origin. The SI unit of position coordinates of the centre of mass is metre (m).
steps: Observe a ceiling fan rotating in your classroom - the entire fan moves as one unit, yet each blade particle follows a different circular path
How do we describe the "overall" motion of such an extended body? We start by recalling from Class 9 (c9_physics_ch2_1) that we treated bodies as point particles located at their geometric centre
But a real cricket bat or a boomerang has mass distributed unevenly
To begin, we pick an origin (say, the corner of the room), measure the position vectors of each mass element, and compute a mass-weighted average position
This average position is the centre of mass - the single point that moves as if all external forces (like gravity) act on the total mass concentrated there
The key formula emerges naturally: R_CM = (Σ m_i r_i) / (Σ m_i).

cards.title: The motion of the centre of mass of a system of particles is governed by the…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: The motion of the centre of mass of a system of particles is governed by the equation \( M \vec{A}_{cm} = \vec{F}_{ext} \), where \( M \) is the total mass of the system, \( \vec{A}_{cm} \) is the acceleration of the centre of mass, and \( \vec{F}_{ext} \) is the vector sum of all external forces acting on the system. The centre of mass moves as if the entire mass of the system were concentrated at that point and all external forces were applied there, regardless of the internal motions or rotations of individual particles.

Surprisingly, the centre of mass of all fragments continues along the original parabolic path as if the explosion never happened

"What forces cause the fragments to fly apart?" (Internal chemical forces)

Emphasise that the summation of internal forces vanishes because they occur in equal and opposite pairs

cards.title: The vector product (cross product) of two vectors a and b is a vector c = a × b…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: The vector product (cross product) of two vectors a and b is a vector c = a × b whose magnitude is |c| = |a||b|sinθ, where θ is the smaller angle (0° ≤ θ ≤ 180°) between a and b, and whose direction is perpendicular to the plane containing a and b following the right-hand screw rule (or right-hand thumb rule). The SI unit of cross product depends on the physical quantities involved (e.g., N·m for torque, kg·m²/s for angular momentum).
steps: Observe a ceiling fan rotating about a vertical axis
When you push a blade tangentially at its outer edge, the fan rotates effectively
Push the same blade near the hinge, and the rotation is negligible
Push radially toward the axis, and there is no rotation at all
This shows that rotational effect depends on (1) the magnitude of force, (2) the distance from the axis, and (3) the sine of the angle between the position vector and force
These three factors combine exactly as the magnitude of a cross product
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., using cosθ, or stating direction is along a or b) reveals confusion between scalar and vector products, or inability to apply the right-hand rule.

cards.title: Torque (or moment of force) is the rotational analogue of force…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Torque (or moment of force) is the rotational analogue of force, defined as the vector product of the position vector r (from the chosen origin to the point of force application) and the force vector F: τ = r × F. Its magnitude is τ = r F sinθ = r⊥ F = r F⊥, where r⊥ is the perpendicular distance from the origin to the line of action of the force (lever arm) and F⊥ is the component of force perpendicular to r. Torque is a vector quantity; its direction is perpendicular to the plane containing r and F, given by the right-hand screw rule. The SI unit of torque is newton metre (N·m), with dimensions [M L² T⁻²].
steps: Observe a ceiling fan in your classroom: when you push the blade near the centre, it barely moves
push at the outer edge, and it spins easily
The turning effect depends on both the force magnitude and where you apply it relative to the axis (hinges)
This is torque

Now, for a force F applied at point P with position vector r from origin O, the torque is τ = r × F

cards.title: Angular momentum (L) of a particle about a point O is the cross product of its…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Angular momentum (L) of a particle about a point O is the cross product of its position vector r (from O to the particle) and its linear momentum p = mv: L = r × p. For a system of particles, total angular momentum is the vector sum L = Σ r_i × p_i. Its SI unit is kg·m²/s. The time rate of change of total angular momentum equals the net external torque: dL/dt = τ_ext. When net external torque is zero, total angular momentum is conserved: L = constant.
steps: Observe a rotating office chair: sit with arms outstretched holding weights, have someone spin you gently, then pull arms in – you spin faster
Start by identifying the system (you + weights + chair)
Ask: what external torques act? Friction at pivot is small but not zero – we approximate it as zero for short durations
The key is recognizing that internal forces (muscles pulling weights) do no net torque
Connect to linear momentum conservation (Class 9): just as F_ext = 0 ⇒ p = constant, here τ_ext = 0 ⇒ L = constant
The formula L = Iω emerges from summing r × (m v) over all particles with v = ω × r.

cards.title: A rigid body is in mechanical equilibrium when both its linear momentum and…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: A rigid body is in mechanical equilibrium when both its linear momentum and angular momentum remain constant with time, which requires the vector sum of all external forces acting on it to be zero (translational equilibrium, ΣF = 0) and the vector sum of all external torques about any point to be zero (rotational equilibrium, Στ = 0). The SI unit for force is newton (N) and for torque is newton-metre (N·m).

To restore balance, you must move your finger toward the coin until the torques balance again

This demonstrates that equilibrium requires both zero net force (your finger pushes up with weight of scale + coin) and zero net torque (clockwise torque = anticlockwise torque about the new support point)

cards.title: The Principle of Moments states that for a rigid body in rotational equilibrium…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: The Principle of Moments states that for a rigid body in rotational equilibrium under the action of coplanar forces, the algebraic sum of the moments (torques) of all forces about any point in the plane is zero; equivalently, the sum of clockwise moments equals the sum of anticlockwise moments about the fulcrum. For a simple lever with two parallel forces F₁ and F₂ perpendicular to the lever arm at distances d₁ and d₂ from the fulcrum, the condition is F₁d₁ = F₂d₂. SI unit of moment is newton-metre (N·m).
steps: Observe a see-saw in a playground: two children of different masses can balance by adjusting their distances from the central pivot
Notice that the heavier child sits closer to the fulcrum
This is the Principle of Moments in action — the product of weight and distance from the pivot must be equal on both sides for balance

cards.title: Moment of inertia (I) of a rigid body about a given axis of rotation is defined…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Moment of inertia (I) of a rigid body about a given axis of rotation is defined as the sum of the products of the masses of all constituent particles and the square of their respective perpendicular distances from that axis. It quantifies the body's resistance to angular acceleration about that axis. For a discrete system: I = Σ m_i r_i²; for a continuous body: I = ∫ r² dm. SI unit: kg·m². Dimensions: [M L² T⁰]. It depends on mass distribution, shape, size, and the choice of rotation axis.
steps: Observe a ceiling fan starting from rest: the blades have the same mass whether stationary or rotating, but the effort needed to spin them up depends on how that mass is distributed relative to the axis
A fan with mass concentrated near the hub spins up faster than one with mass at the blade tips
To quantify this, we first identify the axis of rotation (the motor shaft), then measure each mass element's perpendicular distance to that axis
We square these distances, multiply by respective masses, and sum them
This sum is the moment of inertia
The key insight: it is not mass alone, but mass × (distance)² that determines rotational inertia

cards.title: The Parallel Axis Theorem states that the moment of inertia \(I\) of a rigid…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: The Parallel Axis Theorem states that the moment of inertia \(I\) of a rigid body about any axis is equal to the moment of inertia \(I_{\text{cm}}\) about a parallel axis passing through its centre of mass plus the product of the total mass \(M\) of the body and the square of the perpendicular distance \(d\) between the two parallel axes. Mathematically, \(I = I_{\text{cm}} + M d^2\). The SI unit of moment of inertia is \(\text{kg}\,\text{m}^2\). This theorem applies only when one of the two parallel axes passes through the centre of mass of the body.
steps: Observe a ceiling fan in an Indian household: the blades rotate about the central axis through the motor (centre of mass)
Now imagine the same fan blade detached and rotating about a parallel axis at its edge – like a wheel rotating about a point on its rim
The resistance to rotation (moment of inertia) increases
To quantify this increase, we start from the definition of moment of inertia \(I = \sum m_i r_i^2\) (from node c11_phy_cbse_06_008)
We shift the axis by a distance \(d\) and express the new distances in terms of the old distances from the centre-of-mass axis
Using the definition of centre of mass (\(\sum m_i r_{i,\text{cm}} = 0\)), the cross-term vanishes, leaving the simple additive term \(M d^2\)

cards.title: The Perpendicular Axis Theorem states that for a planar lamina (a thin…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: The Perpendicular Axis Theorem states that for a planar lamina (a thin, flat body), the moment of inertia about an axis perpendicular to its plane is equal to the sum of the moments of inertia about any two mutually perpendicular axes lying in the plane of the lamina and intersecting at the point where the perpendicular axis passes through. Mathematically, if a lamina lies in the xy-plane, then \( I_z = I_x + I_y \), where \( I_z \) is the moment of inertia about the z-axis (perpendicular to the plane), and \( I_x, I_y \) are moments of inertia about the x and y axes in the plane. The SI unit is kg·m². This theorem applies ONLY to planar bodies of negligible thickness.

cards.title: Kinematics of rotational motion describes the motion of a rigid body rotating…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Kinematics of rotational motion describes the motion of a rigid body rotating about a fixed axis using angular displacement (θ), angular velocity (ω), and angular acceleration (α) without considering the forces causing the motion. For constant angular acceleration, the kinematic equations are exact analogues of linear motion equations. Angular displacement is measured in radians (rad), angular velocity in rad/s, and angular acceleration in rad/s².

cards.title: The dynamics of rotational motion about a fixed axis is governed by the…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: The dynamics of rotational motion about a fixed axis is governed by the rotational analogue of Newton's second law: the net external torque (τ) acting on a rigid body equals the product of its moment of inertia (I) about that axis and its angular acceleration (α). Mathematically, τ = Iα. Torque is the rotational analogue of force (SI unit: newton-metre, N·m), moment of inertia is the rotational analogue of mass (SI unit: kg·m²), and angular acceleration is the rate of change of angular velocity (SI unit: rad/s²). This law holds for a rigid body rotating about a fixed axis with constant moment of inertia.

The blades resist this change due to their moment of inertia – a heavy fan accelerates slower than a light one for the same motor torque
This is exactly like pushing a heavy cart (F = ma) but in rotation

cards.title: Rolling motion is the combination of pure translation of the centre of mass and…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Rolling motion is the combination of pure translation of the centre of mass and pure rotation about the centre of mass, where the condition for pure rolling (no slipping) is v_cm = ωR. The total kinetic energy of a body rolling without slipping is the sum of its translational kinetic energy (½mv_cm²) and rotational kinetic energy about the centre of mass (½I_cmω²), giving K_total = ½mv_cm² + ½I_cm(v_cm²/R²) = ½mv_cm²(1 + k²/R²) where k is the radius of gyration about the centre of mass.
