Place a coin on its edge and roll it
the centre translates and the coin rotates simultaneously
The key insight: every point on the rim has velocity v_cm + ω×r relative to centre
For pure rolling, the contact point is instantaneously at rest, so v_cm = ωR

cards.title: Rolling motion on an inclined plane is the combined translational and…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Rolling motion on an inclined plane is the combined translational and rotational motion of a rigid body (cylinder, sphere, ring) moving down a slope under gravity while satisfying the pure rolling condition v = ωR, where the instantaneous point of contact has zero velocity relative to the plane. The linear acceleration of the centre of mass is a = g sinθ / (1 + I/(mR²)), where I is the moment of inertia about the symmetry axis, m is mass, R is radius, and θ is the angle of inclination.

cards.title: Kepler's laws of planetary motion are three empirical principles describing the…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Kepler's laws of planetary motion are three empirical principles describing the motion of planets around the Sun: (1) Law of Orbits – Every planet moves in an elliptical orbit with the Sun at one focus; (2) Law of Areas – The radius vector from the Sun to a planet sweeps out equal areas in equal time intervals, a consequence of angular momentum conservation under a central force; (3) Law of Periods – The square of the orbital period \(T\) is proportional to the cube of the semi-major axis \(a\) of the ellipse, i.e., \(T^2 \propto a^3\). For circular orbits of radius \(r\) around a central mass \(M\), the precise relation is \(T^2 = \frac{4\pi^2}{GM}r^3\), where \(G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11} \, \text{N·m}^2\text{/kg}^2\) is the universal gravitational constant.

cards.title: Newton's Law of Universal Gravitation states that every particle in the…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Newton's Law of Universal Gravitation states that every particle in the universe attracts every other particle with a force that is directly proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between their centres. The force acts along the line joining the two particles and is always attractive. The proportionality constant is the universal gravitational constant \(G\), with a value of \(6.67 \times 10^{-11} \, \text{N m}^2 \text{kg}^{-2}\).
steps: Observe an apple falling from a tree in your school courtyard and the Moon rising in the evening sky
Both are pulled by the Earth, but the Moon doesn't fall down
Start by recalling Kepler's third law from the previous node: \(T^2 \propto r^3\)

Assuming the same force causes both, the force must decrease with distance
Using the known Earth-Moon distance (\(3.84 \times 10^8 \, \text{m}\)) and period (27.3 days), he found \(a_m \approx 0.0027 \, \text{m/s}^2\)

cards.title: The gravitational constant \( G \) is the universal proportionality constant in…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: The gravitational constant \( G \) is the universal proportionality constant in Newton's law of universal gravitation that quantifies the strength of the gravitational force between two point masses. Its experimentally determined value is \( G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11} \, \text{N} \, \text{m}^2 \, \text{kg}^{-2} \). It is a scalar constant that remains invariant across the universe and is measured using a torsion balance (Cavendish experiment) where the tiny gravitational torque between known masses is balanced against the restoring torque of a twisted wire.
steps: Observe that when you bring two large lead spheres near two small spheres on a suspended rod, the rod twists slightly — this is the gravitational force in action, but it is far too weak to measure with a spring balance
Start by recalling Newton's law \( F = G \frac{M m}{d^2} \) from the previous node (c11_phy_cbse_07_002)
The Cavendish apparatus converts this tiny force into a measurable twist angle \( \theta \) using a torsion wire
The key insight is that at equilibrium, the gravitational torque \( F \times L \) equals the restoring torque \( \tau \theta \)
By independently measuring the torsion constant \( \tau \) (using a known torque), we can solve for \( G \)
The critical formula connecting the measurable quantities is \( G = \frac{\tau \theta d^2}{M m L} \).
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., giving \( \text{m/s}^2 \) for \( G \)) reveals the student is confusing the universal constant \( G \) with the local acceleration \( g \), a fundamental category error between a proportionality constant in a force law and an…

cards.title: The acceleration due to gravity (g) at the Earth's surface is the uniform…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: The acceleration due to gravity (g) at the Earth's surface is the uniform acceleration experienced by any freely falling body near the Earth's surface, directed towards the Earth's centre, with magnitude g = GM_E/R_E^2, where G is the universal gravitational constant, M_E is the mass of the Earth, and R_E is the radius of the Earth. Its SI unit is m/s².
steps: Observe a feather and a coin dropped simultaneously in a vacuum tube (or watch a video of Apollo 15 hammer-feather drop on the Moon)
Both hit the ground at the same time, proving acceleration is independent of mass
Now recall Newton's second law: F = ma
The gravitational force on a mass m at Earth's surface is F = GM_Em/R_E^2
Equate the two expressions for force, cancel m, and you get a = GM_E/R_E^2
This acceleration is g
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., g = GM_E/R_E or missing square) reveals the student has not understood the inverse-square law or the derivation from F = GM_Em/R_E^2 = mg.

cards.title: The acceleration due to gravity at a height \(h\) above the Earth's surface is…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: The acceleration due to gravity at a height \(h\) above the Earth's surface is the gravitational acceleration experienced by a point mass at that altitude, given by \(g_h = \frac{GM_E}{(R_E + h)^2}\), where \(G\) is the universal gravitational constant, \(M_E\) is the mass of the Earth, and \(R_E\) is the radius of the Earth. Its SI unit is \(\text{m/s}^2\).
steps: Imagine you are standing on the terrace of a tall building like the Qutub Minar (73 m) and then on the roof of the Burj Khalifa (828 m)
Do you weigh the same? Use a spring balance to measure the weight of a 1 kg mass at ground level and at the top of a tall building — the reading decreases slightly
This happens because gravitational force follows an inverse-square law with distance from Earth's centre
Start by recalling \(g = \frac{GM_E}{R_E^2}\) from the previous node (c11_phy_cbse_07_004)
Replace \(R_E\) with \(R_E + h\) to get the exact formula
Then, for small \(h\) (like mountains, airplanes, low-orbit satellites), use the binomial expansion \((1 + x)^{-2} \approx 1 - 2x\) to obtain the linear approximation \(g_h \approx g(1 - 2h/R_E)\)
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., \(g_h = g - 2gh\) or missing the square) reveals the student has not derived the formula from Newton's law and is memorising incorrectly. They may also confuse the condition with \(h \ll 1\) or not know the binomial expansion condition.

cards.title: The acceleration due to gravity at a depth \(d\) below the Earth's surface…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: The acceleration due to gravity at a depth \(d\) below the Earth's surface, denoted \(g(d)\), is the gravitational acceleration experienced by a test mass at that depth, assuming the Earth is a sphere of uniform density. It is given by \(g(d) = g \left(1 - \frac{d}{R_E}\right)\), where \(g = \frac{GM_E}{R_E^2}\) is the surface value, \(R_E\) is the Earth's radius, and \(d\) is the depth. The SI unit is \(\text{m/s}^2\).
steps: Imagine you are standing at the bottom of a deep mine shaft, say the Kolar Gold Fields in Karnataka, which go down several kilometres
You might wonder: does gravity get stronger because you are closer to the Earth's centre, or weaker because there is less mass below…
The Earth can be thought of as concentric shells
At depth \(d\), the outer shells (thickness \(d\)) exert no force
only the inner sphere of radius \(R_E - d\) matters
Using the mass of this inner sphere and Newton's law, we derive a simple linear relationship.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., \(g(d) = g(1 + d/R_E)\) or \(g(d) = GM_E/(R_E-d)^2\)) reveals the student has not grasped the shell theorem or mistakenly treats the entire Earth's mass as concentrated at the centre even for interior points.

cards.title: The effective acceleration due to gravity (\(g_{\text{eff}}\)) at a point on…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: The effective acceleration due to gravity (\(g_{\text{eff}}\)) at a point on Earth's surface is the vector sum of the true gravitational acceleration (\(g = GM/R^2\), directed toward Earth's centre) and the centrifugal acceleration (\(\omega^2 R \cos\lambda\), directed outward perpendicular to the rotation axis) arising from Earth's rotation. It varies with latitude \(\lambda\) as \(g_{\text{eff}} = g - \omega^2 R \cos^2\lambda\), where \(\omega = 7.292 \times 10^{-5}\,\text{rad/s}\) is Earth's angular speed and \(R = 6.37 \times 10^6\,\text{m}\) is Earth's mean radius.

The centrifugal acceleration \(\omega^2 r\) points outward perpendicular to the axis
Resolve this vector into a component opposite to \(g\) (radial: \(\omega^2 R \cos^2\lambda\)) and a component perpendicular to \(g\) (tangential: \(\omega^2 R \cos\lambda \sin\lambda\))
The radial component reduces the effective weight, giving \(g_{\text{eff}} = g - \omega^2 R \cos^2\lambda\)
The tangential component causes the plumb line to deflect toward the equator.

cards.title: Gravitational potential energy of a system of two point masses is the work done…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Gravitational potential energy of a system of two point masses is the work done by an external agent in assembling them from infinite separation to their current separation, with the zero of potential energy conventionally chosen at infinite separation. It is a scalar quantity measured in joules (J) and is always negative for a bound system, indicating that work must be done to separate the masses to infinity.
steps: Imagine lifting a 1 kg textbook from the classroom floor to a shelf 2 m high
You do work against gravity, storing energy in the book-Earth system
Near Earth's surface, we approximate this as \(mgh\) because gravity is nearly constant
But what if we lift the book to the height of the International Space Station (400 km)? Gravity weakens significantly, so \(mgh\) fails
We must instead calculate the work done against the variable force \(F = \frac{GM_Em}{r^2}\) by integrating from Earth's surface to the final distance
This integration yields the exact formula \(U = -\frac{GM_Em}{r}\), which reduces to \(mgh\) when \(h \ll R_E\)

cards.title: Gravitational potential at a point in a gravitational field is defined as the…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Gravitational potential at a point in a gravitational field is defined as the work done per unit mass in bringing a test mass from infinity to that point without acceleration. It is a scalar quantity denoted by V, with SI unit J/kg (joule per kilogram). For a point mass M, the gravitational potential at distance r is V = -GM/r, where the zero of potential is conventionally chosen at infinity.
steps: Imagine you are standing on the terrace of your school building holding a 1 kg stone

You wonder: "How much energy would I need to give this stone to throw it so far away that Earth's gravity no longer pulls it back?" That energy per kilogram is exactly what gravitational potential measures - but with a…
Start by recalling from Class 9 (c9_physics_ch4_6) that potential energy near Earth's surface is mgh
Now ask: "What happens when we go far from Earth where g is not constant?" This leads to the integral definition W = ∫ F·dr from infinity to r, giving V = -GM/r
Connect this to the previous node c11_phy_cbse_07_008 where we learned gravitational potential energy U = -GMm/r, and see that V = U/m is simply the potential energy per unit mass.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., stating unit as J or N, or calling it a vector) reveals confusion between potential energy (J) and potential (J/kg), or misunderstanding that potential is defined per unit mass, not total energy.

cards.title: Escape velocity is the minimum speed required for an object to escape the…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Escape velocity is the minimum speed required for an object to escape the gravitational influence of a massive body (like Earth) without any further propulsion, reaching infinity with zero residual kinetic energy. Its SI unit is metres per second (m/s). It is derived by equating the initial kinetic energy to the magnitude of the gravitational potential energy at the surface, assuming no non-conservative forces.
steps: Imagine throwing a cricket ball upward from a rooftop in Delhi – it goes up, slows down, and falls back
Now imagine a rocket launched from Sriharikota: with enough initial speed, it never returns
The threshold speed is the escape velocity
To find it, we start with the work-energy theorem: the initial kinetic energy must overcome the negative gravitational potential energy binding the object to Earth
We set the total mechanical energy at launch (surface) equal to the total energy at infinity (zero potential, zero kinetic for minimum speed)
This yields \( \frac{1}{2}mv_e^2 - \frac{GMm}{R} = 0 \), giving \(v_e = \sqrt{2GM/R}\)
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., missing the factor 2, or using \(g\) instead of \(G\)) reveals the student has memorised the formula without understanding its derivation from energy conservation, or confuses escape velocity with orbital velocity (\(v_o = \sqrt{GM/R}\)).

cards.title: Orbital velocity is the minimum horizontal velocity required for a satellite to…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Orbital velocity is the minimum horizontal velocity required for a satellite to maintain a stable circular orbit around Earth at a given altitude, where the gravitational force provides exactly the required centripetal force. The orbital period is the time taken for one complete revolution. For a satellite of mass m in circular orbit at distance r = R_E + h from Earth's centre (R_E = Earth's radius, h = altitude), orbital velocity v = √(GM_E/r) and period T = 2π√(r³/GM_E), where M_E is Earth's mass and G is the gravitational constant. SI units: v in m/s, T in s.
steps: Watch a video of the International Space Station passing overhead — it moves at about 7.7 km/s at 400 km altitude
Notice it doesn't fall down because its horizontal speed is just right: gravity pulls it down, but its inertia carries it forward, so it "falls around" Earth
Start by drawing a free-body diagram: only gravitational force F_g = GM_Em/r² acts, directed toward Earth's centre
This force must equal the required centripetal force m v²/r for circular motion
Equate them, cancel m, and solve for v
Then use v = 2πr/T to find period
cards.misconception: A wrong answer like v = √(2gR_E) reveals confusion with escape velocity; v = gR_E reveals dimensional inconsistency (m²/s² vs m/s); forgetting to convert km to m reveals unit negligence.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: A geostationary satellite orbits Earth in the equatorial plane at an altitude of approximately 35,786 km with a period of exactly 24 hours, matching Earth's rotation so it appears fixed relative to a ground observer. A polar satellite orbits in a near-polar plane at low altitude (500–800 km) with a period of about 100 minutes, passing over the poles on each orbit and scanning the entire Earth's surface as the planet rotates beneath it.

cards.title: Weightlessness in satellites is the condition where an astronaut (or any…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Weightlessness in satellites is the condition where an astronaut (or any object) inside an orbiting satellite experiences zero contact force (normal force) from the satellite surface because both the astronaut and the satellite are in free fall, accelerating towards Earth with the same acceleration g' (acceleration due to gravity at that orbital height). It is a state of apparent weight = 0 N, not the absence of gravitational force.
steps: Imagine standing on a weighing scale in a lift
When the lift cable snaps, the scale reads zero because both you and the lift fall with acceleration g
A satellite is like a lift that never hits the ground — it falls continuously towards Earth but moves forward fast enough to miss it
Both the astronaut and satellite accelerate towards Earth with the same centripetal acceleration g' = GM/(R_E+h)²
Since there is no relative acceleration, the normal force (apparent weight) becomes zero
The key formula is apparent weight = m(g' - a), where a = g' for a freely orbiting satellite.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., stating apparent weight equals mg') reveals confusion between true weight (gravitational force) and apparent weight (contact force), and misunderstanding that weightlessness means zero contact force, not zero gravity.

cards.title: The total mechanical energy of a satellite in a stable orbit around Earth is…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: The total mechanical energy of a satellite in a stable orbit around Earth is the sum of its kinetic energy (due to orbital motion) and gravitational potential energy (due to Earth's gravitational field). For a circular orbit of radius r = Rₑ + h, it is given by E = -GMₑm/(2r), where the negative sign indicates a bound system. The kinetic energy is K = GMₑm/(2r) and potential energy is U = -GMₑm/r, making |U| = 2K and E = -K = U/2.

That horizontal speed is orbital velocity - it's what keeps the satellite "falling around" Earth instead of crashing down

Now ask: what is the satellite's kinetic energy? Substitute v into ½mv² to get K = GMm/(2r)
The potential energy we know from earlier: U = -GMm/r
Add them: E = -GMm/(2r)

cards.title: Stress is the internal restoring force per unit cross-sectional area developed…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Stress is the internal restoring force per unit cross-sectional area developed within a material when an external deforming force is applied, measured in pascals (Pa) or N·m⁻². It quantifies the intensity of internal forces resisting deformation and is a scalar quantity (not a vector) because it acts equally in all directions on a given plane.

Ask: "What invisible force inside the rubber balances the 5 N weight?" Introduce the concept of restoring force per unit area
Connect to Class 9 Newton's third law (action-reaction pairs) and Class 8 pressure (force/area)
Have students press a sponge between palms (compressive stress), pull a spring (tensile), slide a book sideways on a table (shearing), and imagine a balloon underwater (hydraulic)
Derive σ = F/A from the equilibrium condition
Emphasize that stress is defined at a point on a cross-section, not for the whole body.

cards.title: Strain is the dimensionless measure of deformation representing the fractional…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Strain is the dimensionless measure of deformation representing the fractional change in a body's dimension (length, shape, or volume) relative to its original dimension when subjected to a deforming force. It is defined as the ratio of change in dimension to the original dimension, has no SI unit, and is expressed as a pure number or percentage. For a uniform rod under axial force, longitudinal strain = ΔL/L; for tangential force, shearing strain = tan θ ≈ θ (for small θ); for hydraulic pressure, volume strain = ΔV/V.
steps: Observe a rubber band on your desk — when you pull it gently, its length increases from 10 cm to 10.5 cm
The change is visible but small compared to the original length
This fractional change (0.5/10 = 0.05) is the longitudinal strain
Now press a deck of cards sideways — the top cards shift horizontally relative to the bottom
this angular deformation is shearing strain
Finally, imagine a balloon squeezed underwater — its volume decreases uniformly without shape change

cards.title: Hooke's Law states that within the elastic limit of a material…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Hooke's Law states that within the elastic limit of a material, the stress developed is directly proportional to the strain produced. The constant of proportionality is called the modulus of elasticity (or elastic modulus), which characterises the stiffness of the material. Mathematically, stress = E × strain, where E is the modulus of elasticity with SI unit pascal (Pa) or N m⁻².
steps: Imagine stretching a thin steel wire and a rubber band hanging from your classroom ceiling
The steel wire stretches barely a millimetre under a 1 kg load, while the rubber band stretches several centimetres
If you plot the force per unit area (stress) against the fractional elongation (strain) for the steel wire, you get a straight line initially — this is Hooke's law region
For the rubber band, the graph curves upward immediately
In the lab, we use a tensile testing machine to stretch a standardised metal specimen step by step, recording the force and extension at each step
We convert force to stress (F/A) and extension to strain (ΔL/L), then plot stress on the y-axis and strain on the x-axis

remember: State Hooke's law in words and write its mathematical form. What is the name and SI unit of the proportionality constant.

cards.title: The elastic limit is the maximum stress a material can withstand while still…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: The elastic limit is the maximum stress a material can withstand while still returning to its original dimensions upon unloading; the yield point is the specific stress at which a material begins to deform plastically (permanent set) with little or no increase in load. For materials without a distinct yield point, the yield strength is defined as the stress producing a specified permanent strain (typically 0.2%). Both quantities are measured in pascals (Pa) or N/m².
steps: Observe a steel ruler bent slightly — it springs back
bend it further and it stays bent
This everyday observation mirrors the transition from elastic to plastic deformation on a stress-strain curve
Begin by recalling Hooke's law (stress ∝ strain) from the previous node and the definitions of stress (F/A) and strain (ΔL/L)

Plot a few data points from a standard tensile test on mild steel: initially a straight line (OA), then a slight curve (AB) where unloading still returns to zero strain, then a distinct yield point (B) where strain…
Explain that the slope of OA gives Young's modulus, while the stress at B is the yield strength σ_y
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., confusing yield strength with ultimate tensile strength) reveals the student cannot distinguish between the onset of plasticity and the maximum load-bearing capacity.
remember: Define yield strength and state its SI unit. How does it differ from the elastic limit.

cards.title: Young's modulus (Y) is the ratio of longitudinal stress (tensile or…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Young's modulus (Y) is the ratio of longitudinal stress (tensile or compressive) to the corresponding longitudinal strain within the elastic limit of a material. It quantifies the stiffness of a solid material, indicating how much it resists deformation along its length when subjected to an axial force. Its SI unit is pascal (Pa) or N m⁻², and its dimensional formula is [ML⁻¹T⁻²].
steps: Observe a steel ruler clamped at one end on a lab bench
Hang a 500 g mass from the free end — the ruler bends slightly but springs back when the mass is removed
Now try the same with a plastic ruler of the same dimensions — it bends much more
The difference is stiffness, quantified by Young's modulus
Begin by recalling stress = F/A and strain = ΔL/L from previous nodes
The ratio stress/strain gives a material constant Y = (F/A)/(ΔL/L) = FL/(AΔL)
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., Y = FΔL/AL or missing L) reveals the student has not connected the definitions of stress (F/A) and strain (ΔL/L) correctly, or confuses Young's modulus with spring constant k = F/ΔL which depends on geometry.
remember: State the formula for Young's modulus in terms of force (F), original length (L), cross-sectional area (A), and extension (ΔL). Give its SI unit and dimensional formula.

cards.title: Shear modulus (G), also called modulus of rigidity…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Shear modulus (G), also called modulus of rigidity, is the ratio of shearing stress to shearing strain within the elastic limit, measuring a solid's resistance to shape change without volume change; its SI unit is pascal (Pa) or N·m⁻². Bulk modulus (B) is the ratio of hydraulic stress (pressure) to volumetric strain, measuring a material's resistance to uniform compression; its SI unit is also pascal (Pa), with the negative sign in B = -p/(ΔV/V) indicating volume decreases as pressure increases.
steps: Observe a deck of cards on a table: push the top card horizontally while holding the bottom card fixed — the deck tilts like a parallelogram
This is shear deformation: layers slide parallel to each other, changing shape but not volume
Now imagine squeezing a rubber ball uniformly from all sides — it shrinks in volume but stays spherical
This is hydraulic compression
Shear modulus quantifies the first behavior (solids only), bulk modulus quantifies the second (all states of matter)
We begin by identifying the stress type: tangential force per area for shear, normal pressure for bulk
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., giving different units or omitting the negative sign in B) reveals confusion between stress/strain dimensions or misunderstanding that bulk modulus must be positive for stable materials.
remember: State the SI unit of shear modulus and bulk modulus. Are they the same or different? Write the defining formula for each modulus with all variables clearly labeled.

cards.title: Poisson's ratio (σ) is the ratio of lateral strain (fractional change in…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Poisson's ratio (σ) is the ratio of lateral strain (fractional change in diameter perpendicular to applied force) to longitudinal strain (fractional change in length parallel to applied force) within the elastic limit of a material. It is a dimensionless pure number (no units) that characterises how a material contracts laterally when stretched longitudinally. For isotropic materials, its value ranges between 0 and 0.5.
steps: Observe a rubber band being stretched between your fingers — as it gets longer, it visibly becomes thinner
This lateral contraction is not just a rubber phenomenon
a steel wire under tension also contracts in diameter, though the change is too small to see without precise instruments
Start by measuring the original diameter and length of a wire, then apply a known tensile force within the elastic limit and measure the new dimensions
The fractional changes give longitudinal strain (ΔL/L) and lateral strain (Δd/d)
Their ratio defines Poisson's ratio
cards.misconception: A wrong answer of 3.0 or 0.3 without checking physical plausibility reveals the student treats this as pure arithmetic without understanding the physical constraint 0 ≤ σ ≤ 0.5. SI unit: dimensionless (no unit).

cards.title: Elastic potential energy in a stretched wire is the energy stored in a wire…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Elastic potential energy in a stretched wire is the energy stored in a wire when it is deformed within its elastic limit by an external tensile force; it equals the work done by the external force in stretching the wire from its natural length L to L + l and is given by U = ½ × stress × strain × volume = ½ × F × l, where F is the final applied force and l is the total elongation. Its SI unit is joule (J) and it is a scalar quantity.
steps: Imagine a bicycle brake cable being pulled — the lever applies a force that increases from zero to a maximum as the cable stretches

Ask: "If the force varies, how do we calculate the work done?" Connect to Class 9 Work-Energy Theorem (W = ∫F·dx) and the stress-strain curve from c11_phy_cbse_08_004 where the area under the linear O-A region…
Start by measuring the wire's length L, cross-sectional area A, and Young's modulus Y
Then apply the formula U = ½ (YA/L) l² = ½ F l, emphasizing that F is the FINAL force, not the average.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer like U = F l reveals the student incorrectly assumes constant force throughout the elongation, ignoring that the restoring force increases linearly from zero to F. This is the most common error — confusing final force with average force.
remember: State the formula for elastic potential energy stored in a stretched wire in terms of the final tensile force F and the elongation l. What is the SI unit of this energy.
Why is there a factor of ½ in the elastic potential energy formula U = ½ F l, even though work done is generally W = F × displacement.

cards.title: Applications of elastic behaviour involve using the elastic moduli (Young's…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Applications of elastic behaviour involve using the elastic moduli (Young's modulus, shear modulus, bulk modulus) and strength limits (yield strength, ultimate tensile strength) to design load-bearing structures such as beams, columns, ropes, and pillars. The design ensures that operational stresses remain within the elastic limit with a safety factor, preventing permanent deformation or fracture while optimizing material usage and cost.
steps: Observe a construction site where steel ropes lift cement bags and I-beams form the skeleton of a building
Notice the ropes are made of many thin wires braided together, not a single thick rod, and the beams have an I-shaped cross-section
Begin by asking: "Why not use a solid square rod for the…
The key principle is designing dimensions so that maximum operational stress is well below yield strength (safety factor ~10) while minimizing material
The beam depression formula δ = Wl³/(4bd³Y) shows depth d reduces bending more effectively than breadth b, but excessive depth causes buckling — leading to the I-section compromise.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., forgetting the safety factor or using g=10) reveals the student does not understand that the design stress must be a fraction of yield strength, not equal to it, and that safety factors multiply the load, not divide the strength.
remember: A crane is designed to lift a maximum load of 5….

cards.title: The relationship between elastic constants describes the mathematical…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: The relationship between elastic constants describes the mathematical interdependence of Young's modulus (Y), bulk modulus (B), shear modulus (G), and Poisson's ratio (σ) for isotropic materials, allowing any one constant to be determined from the other two. These relations are derived from the generalized Hooke's law for three-dimensional stress states and are valid only within the linear elastic limit.
steps: Observe a rubber eraser being compressed between your fingers — it bulges sideways
This lateral expansion is quantified by Poisson's ratio, which links longitudinal and lateral strains
Start by recalling the three moduli definitions: Y from tensile test, B from hydraulic compression, G from torsion
Then consider a cube under hydrostatic pressure: the volume change gives B, but the same pressure also creates shear distortions on diagonal planes involving G
Equate the strain energy expressions from both perspectives to derive Y = 9BG/(3B+G)
This connects all three moduli through Poisson's ratio σ = (3B-2G)/(6B+2G).
cards.misconception: A wrong answer typically reveals that the student has memorized only one formula (usually Y = 2G(1+σ)) without understanding that any two constants determine the other two, or confuses the formula for plane stress vs. 3D isotropic case.
remember: State the three fundamental relations connecting Young's modulus (Y), bulk modulus (B), shear modulus (G), and Poisson's ratio (σ) for an isotropic material.

cards.title: Pressure is the normal force exerted by a fluid per unit area of the surface in…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Pressure is the normal force exerted by a fluid per unit area of the surface in contact, defined as the limit of the ratio of the normal force ΔF to the area ΔA as the area approaches zero: P = lim(ΔA→0) ΔF/ΔA. It is a scalar quantity with SI unit pascal (Pa) where 1 Pa = 1 N/m², and dimensions [ML⁻¹T⁻²].
steps: Observe a drawing pin pressed into a wall: the sharp tip enters easily while the flat head does not, even with the same force from your thumb
This shows that the effect of force depends on the area over which it acts
In Class 8, you learned pressure = force/area for uniform force
Now we refine this: at a point in a fluid, force may vary across a surface, so we define pressure as the limit of ΔF/ΔA as area shrinks to zero
The force in the numerator is only the component normal to the surface — this is why pressure is scalar, not vector
Start by identifying the normal force component, measure area in m², compute pressure in Pa, then practice converting to atm and bar using 1 atm = 1.013 × 10⁵ Pa.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., giving N/m² without converting to base units, or writing [MLT⁻²]) reveals the student cannot connect derived units to base units or confuse pressure dimensions with force dimensions.
remember: State the SI unit of pressure and its equivalent in base SI units (kg, m, s). Write the dimensional formula of pressure.

cards.title: Pascal's Law states that when an external pressure is applied to an enclosed…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Pascal's Law states that when an external pressure is applied to an enclosed fluid at rest, the pressure change is transmitted undiminished to every point of the fluid and to the walls of the container. The SI unit of pressure is the pascal (Pa), where 1 Pa = 1 N/m².
steps: Observe a hydraulic car lift at a service station: a mechanic applies a small force on a narrow piston, and the platform rises effortlessly lifting a 1500 kg car
Begin by recalling Class 8 pressure definition (P = F/A) and the fact that fluids exert pressure normal to surfaces
Ask: "If I push down on the small piston, how does the large piston 'know' to push up with a larger force?" Guide students to realize the fluid transmits the pressure equally
Connect to the prismatic element proof (NCERT Fig 9.2) where equilibrium of forces on inclined faces leads to Pₐ = P_b = P_c
Conclude with the key hydraulic machine relation: F₁/A₁ = F₂/A₂.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., "pressure is transmitted only downwards" or unit as N/m) reveals confusion between pressure and force, or missing the "enclosed fluid at rest" condition.
remember: State Pascal's Law in one sentence. What is the SI unit of pressure, and what are its base units (kg, m, s).

cards.title: Hydrostatic pressure at a depth \(h\) in a fluid of uniform density \(\rho\) is…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Hydrostatic pressure at a depth \(h\) in a fluid of uniform density \(\rho\) is the normal force per unit area exerted by the fluid column above that point, given by \(P = P_0 + \rho gh\), where \(P_0\) is the pressure at the free surface (often atmospheric pressure), \(g\) is acceleration due to gravity, and \(h\) is the vertical depth measured downward from the free surface. The SI unit is pascal (Pa) or N·m⁻².
steps: Observe a water tank in your home: the tap on the ground floor flows faster than the one on the terrace
This happens because water pressure increases with depth
Begin by drawing a vertical cylindrical fluid element of cross-section \(A\) and height \(h\)
Identify forces: downward force \(P_1A\) on top face, upward force \(P_2A\) on bottom face, and weight \(mg = \rho Ahg\) acting downward
Apply equilibrium condition (net force = 0) to get \((P_2 - P_1)A = \rho Ahg\)
Cancel \(A\) to obtain \(\Delta P = \rho gh\)
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., missing \(P_{\text{atm}}\) or using cm for \(h\)) reveals confusion between gauge and absolute pressure or unit inconsistency.

cards.title: Atmospheric pressure is the pressure exerted by the weight of the air column…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Atmospheric pressure is the pressure exerted by the weight of the air column extending from a point to the top of the atmosphere; at sea level it is 1.013 × 10⁵ Pa (1 atm). Gauge pressure is the difference between the absolute pressure at a point and the local atmospheric pressure (P_gauge = P_absolute − P_atm); it represents the excess pressure over atmospheric pressure. Both are scalar quantities measured in pascals (Pa = N/m²).
steps: Observe a drinking straw: when you suck, you reduce the pressure inside your mouth, and the atmospheric pressure pushing down on the liquid surface in the glass forces the liquid up the straw
This shows atmospheric pressure acts in all directions and can support a liquid column
Recall from the previous node (Variation of Pressure with Depth) that pressure at depth h in a liquid open to atmosphere is P = P_atm + ρgh
The extra pressure ρgh is exactly the gauge pressure
Introduce the mercury barometer: an inverted tube filled with mercury creates a vacuum at the top
the mercury column falls until its weight is balanced by atmospheric pressure on the reservoir surface, giving P_atm = ρ_Hg g h_Hg
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., giving the unit as N/m or stating the value as 1.013 × 10⁵ N/m² without the exponent) reveals confusion between pressure and force, or inability to handle scientific notation and units correctly.
remember: Define atmospheric pressure and state its SI unit. What is the standard value of atmospheric pressure at sea level in pascals.

cards.title: A hydraulic machine is a device that uses an incompressible fluid to transmit…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: A hydraulic machine is a device that uses an incompressible fluid to transmit pressure undiminished from a small piston to a larger piston, multiplying the applied force in proportion to the ratio of their cross-sectional areas, as a direct consequence of Pascal's law for enclosed fluids at rest.
steps: Observe a car being lifted at a service station: a mechanic pushes a small pedal, and a massive car rises smoothly
This is a hydraulic lift
Start by recalling Pascal's law: pressure applied to an enclosed fluid transmits equally in all directions
Connect to the earlier node on Pascal's law (c11_phy_cbse_09_002)
Imagine two syringes of different sizes connected by a tube filled with water
Push the smaller piston — the larger one moves out with greater force but smaller displacement
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., F₂ = F₁) reveals the student thinks force is transmitted directly, not pressure, confusing Newton's third law with hydraulic transmission.
remember: State Pascal's law as applied to hydraulic machines and write the formula relating the forces on two pistons of areas A₁ and A₂ in a hydraulic lift.

cards.title: Archimedes' principle states that when a body is partially or fully immersed in…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Archimedes' principle states that when a body is partially or fully immersed in a fluid at rest, it experiences an upward buoyant force equal in magnitude to the weight of the fluid displaced by the immersed portion of the body. The buoyant force acts vertically upward through the centre of gravity of the displaced fluid (centre of buoyancy). SI unit of buoyant force is newton (N). For a fluid of density ρ_f, the buoyant force on a volume V_submerged is F_b = ρ_f V_submerged g.
steps: Begin with a familiar observation: when you push an empty plastic mug into a bucket of water, you feel a strong upward push resisting your hand
Ask: "Where does this upward force come from?" Guide the student to recall that pressure in a fluid increases with depth (c11_phy_cbse_09_003)
The pressure on the bottom surface of the mug is greater than on the top surface, creating a net upward force
Now imagine replacing the mug with a water-filled mug of the same shape – the water inside would be in equilibrium, so the net upward force on it must exactly balance its weight
This upward force is the buoyant force, and it equals the weight of the displaced fluid
The key formula F_b = ρ_f V_displaced g emerges directly from the pressure-depth relationship.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., F_b = ρ_object V g) reveals the student confuses the density of the object with the density of the fluid – a fundamental category error.

cards.title: Bernoulli's principle states that for a steady, incompressible…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Bernoulli's principle states that for a steady, incompressible, non-viscous fluid flow along a streamline, the sum of pressure energy per unit volume (P), kinetic energy per unit volume (½ρv²), and potential energy per unit volume (ρgh) remains constant. Mathematically, P + ½ρv² + ρgh = constant, where P is pressure (Pa), ρ is fluid density (kg/m³), v is flow speed (m/s), g is acceleration due to gravity (m/s²), and h is height above a reference level (m).
steps: Observe water flowing from a garden hose: when you partially cover the opening with your thumb, the water jets out faster and travels farther
This everyday observation connects to the equation of continuity (Av = constant) learned in c11_phy_cbse_09_003 - as area decreases, velocity must increase
But what happens to pressure? Recall from c9_physics_ch4_8 that energy is conserved
The work done by pressure forces on a fluid element equals its change in kinetic and potential energy
Begin by considering a fluid element moving from a wide section to a narrow section of a horizontal pipe
Identify the forces (pressure at both ends), calculate work done, equate to ΔK + ΔU, and derive the relationship

cards.title: Bernoulli's principle states that for an incompressible…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Bernoulli's principle states that for an incompressible, non-viscous fluid in steady streamline flow, the sum of pressure energy per unit volume (P), kinetic energy per unit volume (½ρv²), and potential energy per unit volume (ρgh) remains constant along a streamline. Its applications include Torricelli's law for efflux speed, dynamic lift on aerofoils and spinning balls (Magnus effect), and Venturi meter for flow measurement.
steps: Observe a garden hose: when you partially block the nozzle with your thumb, water jets out faster and reaches farther
This is Bernoulli's principle in action — constriction increases speed, decreasing pressure

cards.title: The coefficient of viscosity (η) is a scalar physical quantity that measures a…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: The coefficient of viscosity (η) is a scalar physical quantity that measures a fluid's internal resistance to flow by quantifying the ratio of shearing stress to the rate of shearing strain. For a fluid layer of area A moving with velocity v relative to a parallel stationary layer separated by distance l, η = (F/A) / (v/l) = Fl/(Av), where F is the tangential force required to maintain the motion. Its SI unit is pascal-second (Pa·s) or N·s·m⁻², with dimensions [ML⁻¹T⁻¹].
steps: Observe honey dripping slowly from a spoon versus water flowing rapidly from a tap — both are liquids but resist flow differently
This resistance arises because adjacent fluid layers exert tangential forces on each other
To quantify this, imagine two horizontal glass plates with a liquid film between them: the bottom plate is fixed, the top plate moves at constant velocity v
The liquid layer touching the top plate moves at v (no-slip condition), while the layer touching the bottom plate is stationary
Assuming a linear velocity profile, the velocity gradient is v/l
The force F needed to pull the top plate at constant speed is proportional to area A and velocity gradient
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., Poise without conversion, or [ML⁻¹T⁻²]) reveals confusion between viscosity and pressure, or between dynamic and kinematic viscosity.

cards.title: Stokes' Law states that the viscous drag force \(F\) on a small sphere of…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Stokes' Law states that the viscous drag force \(F\) on a small sphere of radius \(a\) moving with velocity \(v\) through a fluid of coefficient of viscosity \(\eta\) under laminar flow conditions is \(F = 6\pi\eta a v\). Terminal velocity \(v_t\) is the constant maximum velocity attained by a falling sphere when the net force becomes zero: \(v_t = \frac{2a^2(\rho - \sigma)g}{9\eta}\), where \(\rho\) is the density of the sphere, \(\sigma\) is the density of the fluid, and \(g\) is acceleration due to gravity.
steps: Watch a raindrop falling on a window pane during monsoon — it doesn't accelerate indefinitely but reaches a steady speed
This is terminal velocity
Begin by recalling viscosity (c11_phy_cbse_09_009): adjacent fluid layers exert shear forces proportional to velocity gradient
Now imagine a small steel ball dropped in a tall cylinder of glycerine
Initially gravity accelerates it, but as speed increases, viscous drag grows linearly with velocity (Stokes' Law)
Simultaneously, Archimedes' principle gives an upward buoyant force
cards.misconception: A wrong answer missing any condition reveals the student thinks Stokes' Law applies universally to all falling objects, ignoring the laminar flow requirement.

cards.title: Reynolds number (Re) is a dimensionless quantity that predicts the flow regime…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Reynolds number (Re) is a dimensionless quantity that predicts the flow regime of a fluid by comparing inertial forces to viscous forces, defined as Re = ρvD/η where ρ is fluid density (kg/m³), v is characteristic flow velocity (m/s), D is characteristic linear dimension such as pipe diameter (m), and η is dynamic viscosity (Pa·s); for pipe flow, laminar flow occurs when Re < 2000, transitional flow when 2000 < Re < 4000, and turbulent flow when Re > 4000.
steps: Open a tap slowly and observe the smooth, glassy water stream — this is laminar flow where fluid particles move in parallel layers
Now open the tap fully
the stream becomes chaotic, foamy, and noisy — this is turbulent flow with eddies and mixing
The transition happens at a critical speed that depends on the fluid's viscosity and density, and the pipe diameter
We quantify this using Reynolds number, a ratio of inertial forces (ρv²) that promote chaotic motion to viscous forces (ηv/D) that resist it

cards.title: Surface tension is the property of a liquid surface to behave like a stretched…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Surface tension is the property of a liquid surface to behave like a stretched elastic membrane due to cohesive forces between molecules, quantified as the force acting per unit length of an imaginary line drawn on the surface (SI unit: N/m) or equivalently the surface energy per unit area (SI unit: J/m²). It arises because molecules at the interface have higher potential energy than those in the bulk.
steps: Observe a steel needle floating on water in a bowl — it depresses the surface but doesn't sink
This happens because the water surface acts like a stretched membrane pulling upward along the contact line
Start by asking: "What force balances the needle's weight?" Guide students to realize the surface pulls tangentially along the contact perimeter
Connect to Class 9 work-energy (c9_physics_ch4_1): stretching the surface by moving a slider on a wire frame does work against surface tension, storing energy
Define surface tension S = F/l = dW/dA
Derive excess pressure by equating work done by pressure difference (ΔP × dV) to increase in surface energy (S × dA) for a spherical drop and bubble.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., calling it a vector or giving only N/m) reveals confusion between force direction and the scalar property of the interface.
remember: Define surface tension and state its two equivalent SI units. Why is surface tension a scalar quantity despite being defined as force per unit length.

cards.title: Capillary rise is the phenomenon where a liquid ascends or descends in a narrow…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Capillary rise is the phenomenon where a liquid ascends or descends in a narrow tube (capillary) due to the pressure difference across a curved meniscus caused by surface tension. The ascent formula \( h = \frac{2S \cos\theta}{\rho g r} \) gives the equilibrium height \( h \) (m) of the liquid column, where \( S \) is the surface tension (N/m), \( \theta \) is the contact angle (rad or °), \( \rho \) is the liquid density (kg/m³), \( g \) is acceleration due to gravity (m/s²), and \( r \) is the internal radius of the capillary tube (m). The formula assumes a uniform cylindrical tube, a hemispherical meniscus, and negligible tube length compared to the reservoir.
steps: Observe a glass thermometer or a thin straw dipped in water: the water climbs up the tube, defying gravity
This is capillary rise
Now dip the same tube in mercury: the mercury level goes down inside the tube
Why? Recall from c11_phy_cbse_09_012 that a curved liquid surface creates a pressure difference \( \Delta P = \frac{2S}{R} \) (Laplace pressure)
The meniscus curvature radius \( R \) relates to the tube radius \( r \) by \( R = \frac{r}{\cos\theta} \) (from c11_phy_cbse_09_014)
At the meniscus (point A), the pressure on the liquid side is lower than atmospheric for a concave meniscus (water) and higher for a convex meniscus (mercury)
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., using \( \sin\theta \) or omitting \( \cos\theta \)) reveals the student memorized the formula without understanding the geometric projection of the meniscus curvature onto the tube axis.
remember: State the capillary ascent formula and define each variable with its SI unit. Why does the formula contain \( \cos\theta \) instead of \( \sin\theta \) or \( \theta \) directly.

cards.title: The angle of contact (θ) is the angle measured inside the liquid between the…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: The angle of contact (θ) is the angle measured inside the liquid between the tangent to the liquid-air interface at the point of contact and the solid surface. It quantifies the balance of interfacial tensions at the three-phase boundary (solid-liquid-air) and determines whether a liquid wets a solid (θ < 90°, concave meniscus) or does not wet it (θ > 90°, convex meniscus). Its SI unit is degree (°) or radian (rad), though it is a dimensionless geometric angle.
steps: Observe a glass of water and a glass of mercury side by side: the water surface curves upward at the edges (concave meniscus) while mercury curves downward (convex meniscus)
This difference arises from how strongly liquid molecules attract the solid compared to each other
Begin by drawing the three interfacial tensions (solid-air, solid-liquid, liquid-air) acting at the contact line on a diagram
Resolve the liquid-air tension along the solid surface to obtain Young's equation: S_la cos θ = S_sa - S_sl
If S_sa > S_sl, cos θ is positive → θ < 90° (acute) → liquid spreads/wets
If S_sa < S_sl, cos θ is negative → θ > 90° (obtuse) → liquid beads up
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., measuring the angle outside the liquid, or confusing θ with the angle of the meniscus curvature) reveals the student has not internalised the precise geometric definition and the convention of measuring inside the liquid.
remember: Define angle of contact and state its SI unit. Draw a labeled diagram showing the angle of contact for a liquid that wets the solid (θ < 90°) and one that does not wet (θ > 90°).
Using Young's equation (S_la cos θ = S_sa - S_sl), explain why a liquid with θ > 90° does not wet the solid….

cards.title: Temperature is an intensive thermodynamic quantity that quantifies the degree…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Temperature is an intensive thermodynamic quantity that quantifies the degree of hotness of a body on a numerical scale; it determines the direction of heat flow when two systems are in thermal contact. Heat is energy in transit transferred between a system and its surroundings solely due to a temperature difference; it is not a property contained within a body. The SI unit of temperature is kelvin (K) and of heat is joule (J).
steps: Place a steel spoon and a wooden spoon in a mug of hot tea
After 30 seconds, touch both handles — the steel spoon feels much hotter
Both spoons are at the same temperature (thermal equilibrium with the tea), yet they transfer heat to your hand at different rates
This shows temperature alone does not determine how much heat flows
material properties matter

Begin by asking: "If both spoons are at the same temperature, why does one burn your hand faster?" This leads to the key principle: temperature indicates direction of heat flow (from hot to cold), while heat is the…
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., "heat is energy stored in a body") reveals the caloric theory misconception where students treat heat as a fluid-like substance contained within objects.
remember: Define temperature and heat. State their SI units. Is heat a property of a system? Justify your answer in one sentence.

cards.title: Temperature is a scalar physical quantity that quantifies the degree of hotness…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Temperature is a scalar physical quantity that quantifies the degree of hotness or coldness of a body on a defined scale; it is measured using a thermometric property (such as volume of a liquid, pressure of a gas, or electrical resistance) that varies monotonically with temperature. The SI unit of temperature is the kelvin (K), defined such that the triple point of water is exactly 273.16 K; the Celsius scale (°C) is related by t/°C = T/K – 273.15, and the Fahrenheit scale (°F) by t/°F = (9/5) t/°C + 32.
steps: Observe a clinical mercury thermometer and a laboratory Celsius thermometer side by side: both use mercury expansion but have different scale markings
Ask: "If the mercury thread stands at the same height in both, why do they read different numbers?" This leads to the realisation that scales are human conventions anchored to fixed points

Begin by identifying the two historical fixed points — ice point (melting ice at 1 atm) and steam point (boiling water at 1 atm) — and assign them arbitrary numbers (0 and 100 for Celsius, 32 and 212 for Fahrenheit)
Show that a linear relationship between the scales follows from the assumption that the thermometric property varies linearly with temperature
Derive the conversion formula tF = (9/5)tC + 32 by equating the fraction of the interval between fixed points
Then introduce the constant-volume gas thermometer: plot pressure vs
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., 273 K for ice point, or 100 K for steam point) reveals that the student has memorised the Celsius values but not the Kelvin offsets, or confuses the triple point (273.16 K) with the ice point (273.15 K).
remember: State the exact numerical values (with units) of the ice point and steam point on the Celsius, Fahrenheit, and Kelvin scales.
Explain why the Kelvin scale is called an "absolute" temperature scale, whereas Celsius and Fahrenheit are "relative" scales. Use the ideal gas law in your reasoning.

cards.title: Linear thermal expansion is the increase in length of a solid rod or wire when…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Linear thermal expansion is the increase in length of a solid rod or wire when its temperature rises, quantified by the coefficient of linear expansion αₗ (SI unit: K⁻¹), defined as the fractional change in length per unit temperature change: αₗ = (1/l)(Δl/ΔT) for small ΔT, where l is the original length at reference temperature.
steps: Observe a metal lid stuck on a glass pickle jar — when you run hot water over the lid, it loosens
This happens because the metal (αₗ ≈ 1.7×10⁻⁵ K⁻¹ for brass) expands more than glass (αₗ ≈ 0.32×10⁻⁵ K⁻¹)
Start by identifying the three quantities: original length l, temperature change ΔT, and material's αₗ from Table 10.1
The key insight is that Δl is proportional to both l and ΔT, so a 1 m rod expands 10× more than a 10 cm rod for the same ΔT
Connect to Class 10's "Heat vs Temperature" (c10_phy_cbse_03_001): temperature change drives the expansion, not the absolute temperature
The governing formula Δl = αₗ l ΔT emerges directly from the definition αₗ = (Δl/l)/ΔT.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer of 0.36 mm indicates a decimal error (forgetting 1000 mm/m); 36 mm indicates using ΔT = 250 K instead of 25 K.
remember: State the SI unit of coefficient of linear expansion αₗ and write its defining formula in terms of Δl, l, and ΔT.

cards.title: The coefficient of area expansion (β) is defined as the fractional increase in…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: The coefficient of area expansion (β) is defined as the fractional increase in area per unit rise in temperature: β = (1/A)(ΔA/ΔT). The coefficient of volume expansion (γ) is defined as the fractional increase in volume per unit rise in temperature: γ = (1/V)(ΔV/ΔT). Both have SI unit K⁻¹ (or °C⁻¹). For isotropic solids, β = 2α and γ = 3α, where α is the coefficient of linear expansion.
steps: Observe a metal jar lid that is stuck: running hot water over the lid (not the glass) loosens it because the metal lid expands more in area than the glass threads
To analyse this, start with a rectangular sheet of length L and breadth B at temperature T
When heated by ΔT, each linear dimension increases by ΔL = αLΔT and ΔB = αBΔT
The new area is (L+ΔL)(B+ΔB) = LB + LΔB + BΔL + ΔLΔB
The product ΔLΔB is of order (αΔT)² and is negligible for small ΔT (α ~ 10⁻⁵ K⁻¹)
Thus ΔA ≈ LΔB + BΔL = 2αABΔT, giving β = 2α
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., γ = α or γ = α³) reveals the student has not understood the geometric derivation from linear expansion or is confusing volume expansion with linear expansion.
remember: Define the coefficient of volume expansion (γ) and state its SI unit. How is it related to the coefficient of linear expansion (α) for an isotropic solid.

cards.title: Anomalous expansion of water is the phenomenon where water contracts on heating…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Anomalous expansion of water is the phenomenon where water contracts on heating between 0°C and 4°C, reaching its maximum density of approximately 1000 kg/m³ at 4°C, and expands on further heating above 4°C. This behavior is opposite to the typical thermal expansion of liquids and is due to the hydrogen-bonded network structure of water.
steps: Begin by showing a video or image of a frozen lake in Ladakh or Kashmir with fish swimming underneath the ice
Ask: "Why doesn't the entire lake freeze solid, killing all aquatic life?" Guide students to recall that solids are usually denser than liquids, so they sink
Then reveal that ice floats because water expands on freezing
Now ask: "What happens to water density as it cools from 10°C to 0°C?" Most students will say density increases monotonically
Show the temperature–density graph (Fig 10.7 in NCERT) and highlight the peak at 4°C
Connect this to the convection currents in a cooling lake: water at 4°C sinks, while colder water stays on top and freezes
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., 0°C or 100°C) reveals that the student has not internalized the anomalous peak and still assumes density increases monotonically with cooling, confusing water with typical liquids.
remember: State the temperature at which water has its maximum density and the corresponding density value in SI units.
Explain why a lake freezes from the top surface downward rather than from the bottom up, using the concept of density variation with temperature.

cards.title: Specific heat capacity is the amount of heat energy required to raise the…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Specific heat capacity is the amount of heat energy required to raise the temperature of one kilogram of a substance by one kelvin (or one degree Celsius) without any change of state. It is an intrinsic property of the material, denoted by s (or c), with SI unit J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹. Mathematically, s = (1/m)(ΔQ/ΔT) where m is mass, ΔQ is heat supplied, and ΔT is temperature change.
steps: Observe a steel spoon and a wooden spoon left in a hot cup of tea — the steel spoon becomes too hot to touch much faster than the wooden one, even though both absorb heat from the same tea
This happens because steel requires less heat per kilogram to raise its temperature
Begin by recalling that heat (ΔQ) depends on mass (m) and temperature change (ΔT) from Class 10

Introduce the proportionality constant 's' that captures the material's "thermal inertia." Connect to the prior node on Temperature and Heat Distinction (c11_phy_cbse_10_001) where heat was defined as energy transfer…
Derive s = ΔQ/(mΔT) and emphasize that 's' is independent of mass but depends on the substance's nature.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer like J K⁻¹ reveals confusion between heat capacity (S) and specific heat capacity (s) — the student omitted the per-unit-mass…
remember: State the SI unit of specific heat capacity and write its dimensional formula.

A 0.5 kg aluminium block (s = 900 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹) is heated from 27°C to 77°C. Calculate the heat energy supplied in kJ.

cards.title: Molar specific heat capacity is the amount of heat energy required to raise the…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Molar specific heat capacity is the amount of heat energy required to raise the temperature of one mole of a substance by one kelvin (or one degree Celsius). It is denoted by \(C\) and its SI unit is \(\text{J mol}^{-1} \text{K}^{-1}\). For gases, two distinct values are defined: molar specific heat at constant pressure (\(C_p\)) and molar specific heat at constant volume (\(C_v\)), because the heat supplied is partly used for expansion work at constant pressure.
steps: Observe a domestic LPG cylinder: we purchase gas by mass (kg), but chemists and physicists often quantify it in moles for thermodynamic calculations
Recall from the previous node (Specific Heat Capacity) that water requires 4186 J per kg per K
Now ask: "How much heat for one mole of water?" This shifts the basis from mass to amount of substance
Connect to the mole concept from chemistry: one mole of any substance contains Avogadro's number of particles
Define molar specific heat capacity as heat per mole per kelvin
For gases, demonstrate with a syringe: compressing the gas (constant volume) vs
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., giving \(\text{J kg}^{-1} \text{K}^{-1}\)) reveals confusion between specific heat capacity (per unit mass) and molar specific heat capacity (per unit amount of substance).
remember: State the definition of molar specific heat capacity and its SI unit.
Why do gases have two molar specific heat capacities (\(C_p\) and \(C_v\)) while solids and liquids are usually described by only one.

cards.title: Calorimetry is the experimental technique of measuring heat transfer between…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Calorimetry is the experimental technique of measuring heat transfer between bodies in an isolated system based on the principle of conservation of energy: the total heat lost by hotter bodies equals the total heat gained by colder bodies, assuming no heat exchange with the surroundings. The device used is a calorimeter (typically a copper or aluminium vessel with a stirrer, insulated by a wooden jacket containing glass wool). The SI unit of heat measured is joule (J).
steps: Imagine placing a hot samosa on a cold plate – the samosa cools while the plate warms until both reach the same temperature
This everyday heat exchange is the heart of calorimetry
Begin by identifying all objects in the isolated system (hot body, cold water, calorimeter cup, stirrer)
List their masses, initial temperatures, and known specific heat capacities
The final equilibrium temperature is the single unknown that links all heat transfers
Apply the conservation equation: Σ mᵢ sᵢ (T_f - T_i) = 0, where heat lost (negative ΔT) balances heat gained (positive ΔT)
cards.misconception: A wrong answer like "m₁ s₁ T₁ = m₂ s₂ T₂" reveals the student ignores temperature change and uses absolute temperatures, confusing heat content with heat transfer.
remember: State the principle of calorimetry and write the mathematical equation representing it for a system of two bodies with masses m₁, m₂, specific heats s₁, s₂, initial temperatures….
A student claims: "In a calorimeter experiment, the heat lost by the hot metal block is exactly equal to the heat gained by the water alone." Explain why this statement is….

cards.title: Change of state is a physical process where matter transitions between solid…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Change of state is a physical process where matter transitions between solid, liquid, and gas phases due to heat exchange at constant temperature and pressure. Melting (fusion) is the solid-to-liquid transition at the melting point; boiling (vaporisation) is the liquid-to-gas transition at the boiling point. During these transitions, the temperature remains constant while heat energy (latent heat) is absorbed or released to overcome intermolecular forces.
steps: Observe an ice cube melting in a glass of water at room temperature — the ice stays at 0°C until fully melted, even though the surroundings are warmer
This shows temperature is constant during phase change
Start by recalling that heat usually raises temperature (specific heat capacity)
Now ask: what happens when heat is supplied but temperature doesn't rise? The energy goes into breaking intermolecular bonds, not increasing kinetic energy
Demonstrate with a temperature-time graph for heating ice: flat regions at 0°C (melting) and 100°C (boiling)
Connect to pressure effects: pressure cooker raises boiling point
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., "melting point is when ice turns to water at 0°C only") reveals the student thinks these are fixed values independent of pressure, missing the pressure-dependence central to senior secondary physics.
remember: Define melting point and boiling point. State their SI units and how they differ from normal melting/boiling points.
Why does the temperature of a substance remain constant during melting or boiling even though heat is continuously supplied? Explain at the molecular level.
Calculate the heat required to melt 250 g of ice at 0°C completely into water at 0°C. Given latent heat of fusion of ice Lf = 3.34 × 10⁵ J/kg.

cards.title: Latent heat is the amount of heat energy per unit mass absorbed or released by…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Latent heat is the amount of heat energy per unit mass absorbed or released by a substance during a change of state at constant temperature and pressure. The latent heat of fusion (L_f) is for solid-liquid transition, and latent heat of vaporisation (L_v) is for liquid-gas transition. Its SI unit is joule per kilogram (J kg⁻¹).
steps: Observe a pressure cooker whistling: water boils at 100°C but the temperature stays constant while steam forms
Ask why the temperature doesn't rise even though the flame supplies heat
Connect to the Class 10 observation that ice melts at 0°C without temperature change
Introduce the idea that heat is used to overcome intermolecular forces, not increase kinetic energy
Define latent heat as the "hidden" heat for phase change
Derive Q = mL from the proportionality of heat to mass
cards.misconception: A wrong answer like "J" or "J/kg·K" reveals confusion between latent heat and specific heat capacity, or missing the per-unit-mass nature of latent heat.
remember: State the SI unit of latent heat and write the formula relating heat supplied (Q), mass (m), and latent heat (L) for a phase change.
Explain why the temperature of a substance remains constant during melting even though heat is continuously supplied. What happens to the supplied energy at the molecular level.
Calculate the heat required to convert 50 g of ice at 0°C to water at 0°C. Latent heat of fusion of ice = 3.33 × 10⁵ J kg⁻¹.

cards.title: Conduction is the mode of heat transfer between adjacent parts of a material…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Conduction is the mode of heat transfer between adjacent parts of a material due to a temperature gradient, where energy is transferred through molecular collisions and lattice vibrations without any bulk motion of the material. The rate of heat flow (heat current) H in steady state through a uniform rod of length L, cross-sectional area A, with ends maintained at temperatures T_H (hot) and T_C (cold) is given by H = K A (T_H - T_C) / L, where K is the thermal conductivity of the material (SI unit: W m⁻¹ K⁻¹).
steps: Place a metal spoon and a wooden spoon in a hot cup of tea
Within seconds, the metal spoon's handle becomes too hot to touch, while the wooden spoon remains comfortable
This immediate, observable difference is conduction: metals have high thermal conductivity (K ~ 100-400 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹) while wood has low K (~ 0.1-0.2 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹)
Start by identifying the temperature difference as the driving force, the geometry (L, A) as the path, and K as the material property
Connect to the prior concept of heat current (H = dQ/dt) from calorimetry
The key principle: in steady state, heat current is constant along the rod, so H₁ = H₂ at any junction, allowing you to solve for unknown junction temperatures.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., unit as W m⁻¹ or J K⁻¹) reveals confusion between thermal conductivity and thermal conductance, or missing the area/length dependence.
remember: State the SI unit of thermal conductivity and write the defining formula for heat current H through a rod in steady state, defining each symbol.

cards.title: Thermal conductivity (K) is a material property that quantifies the ability of…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Thermal conductivity (K) is a material property that quantifies the ability of a substance to conduct heat, defined as the rate of heat flow per unit area per unit temperature gradient under steady-state conditions. Its SI unit is W m⁻¹ K⁻¹ (or J s⁻¹ m⁻¹ K⁻¹). Thermal resistance (R) is the reciprocal measure of a material's opposition to heat flow, given by R = L/(KA) for a slab of length L and cross-sectional area A, with SI unit K W⁻¹.
steps: Touch a metal spoon and a wooden spoon left in a hot cup of tea - the metal feels much hotter because it conducts heat faster to your fingers
This everyday observation reveals that materials differ in their ability to transfer heat
To quantify this, we consider a uniform rod with ends at different temperatures and measure how much heat flows per second
The key insight is that in steady state, the heat current (rate of heat flow) must be the same through every cross-section, just like electric current in a series circuit
This analogy with electrical resistance (Class 10, Chapter 12) lets us define thermal resistance R = L/KA and treat composite rods as series resistors
The formula H = KA(ΔT)/L emerges from Fourier's law of conduction, where H is heat current in watts.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer like H = 343 W reveals missing unit conversion (cm² to m²). Getting T_j = 31.5°C means the student subtracted from the cold end instead of the hot end.
remember: State the SI unit of thermal conductivity and write the formula for heat current through a uniform rod of length L, cross-sectional area A, thermal conductivity K, with its ends….
Two rods of identical dimensions but different materials (copper and steel) are joined….
A brass rod (K = 109 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹) of length 20 cm and cross-section 2 cm² is joined to a steel rod (K = 50 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹) of length 30 cm and cross-section 3….

cards.title: Convection is a mode of heat transfer in fluids (liquids and gases) where…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Convection is a mode of heat transfer in fluids (liquids and gases) where thermal energy is transported by the bulk motion of the fluid itself, driven by density differences arising from temperature gradients. It occurs only in fluids because solids cannot flow. The SI unit for the rate of heat transfer by convection is the watt (W).
steps: Observe a pot of water heating on a stove: bubbles form at the bottom and rise vigorously, while the water appears to circulate
This is convection in action
Now, recall from Class 9 that fluids expand when heated (thermal expansion), becoming less dense
Because of gravity, the buoyant force pushes this lighter fluid upward, while denser, cooler fluid sinks to take its place
This creates a continuous cycle called a convection current
Start by identifying the heat source and the resulting density gradient
cards.misconception: A wrong answer stating "convection occurs in solids" or "convection does not need gravity" reveals a confusion with conduction or a misunderstanding of the buoyancy-driven mechanism.
remember: What is the fundamental requirement for natural convection to occur in a fluid.
Why does a convection current stop if a fluid is heated uniformly from all sides (or from the top) instead of from below.
A room heater with a fan (forced convection) warms a 20 m² room in 15….

cards.title: Stefan-Boltzmann law states that the total radiant energy emitted per unit time…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Stefan-Boltzmann law states that the total radiant energy emitted per unit time (power radiated) by a perfect blackbody is directly proportional to the fourth power of its absolute temperature and its surface area, given by H = AσT⁴, where σ = 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ W m⁻² K⁻⁴ is the Stefan-Boltzmann constant. For real bodies with emissivity e (0 < e ≤ 1), the radiated power is H = AeσT⁴.
steps: Stand near a traditional clay tandoor (oven) in a North Indian dhaba — you feel intense heat on your face even before hot air reaches you
This is radiation: energy travelling as electromagnetic waves without heating the air in between
Recall from Class 7 that black surfaces absorb/emit better
now we quantify it
First, measure the tandoor's outer surface temperature (say 500 °C = 773 K) and estimate its area
Then use Stefan's law H = AeσT⁴ to find radiative power
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., H ∝ T² or σ in J instead of W) reveals confusion between energy and power, or misunderstanding that radiation depends on the fourth power of absolute temperature, not Celsius.
remember: State the Stefan-Boltzmann law for a perfect blackbody and give the SI unit and value of the Stefan-Boltzmann constant σ.
A student claims: "If I double the Celsius temperature of a hot plate from 100 °C to 200 °C, its radiative power increases by 2⁴ = 16 times." Identify the error and calculate the….
A spherical clay pot (emissivity e = 0.9, radius 0.15 m) at 400 °C is kept in a room at 27 °C. Calculate the net radiative heat loss rate. Use σ = 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ W m⁻² K⁻⁴.

cards.title: Newton's Law of Cooling states that the rate of heat loss from a body is…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Newton's Law of Cooling states that the rate of heat loss from a body is directly proportional to the temperature difference between the body and its surroundings, provided the temperature difference is small (typically less than 30°C). The law applies to combined heat transfer by conduction, convection, and radiation. The rate of cooling is given by -dQ/dt = k(T - Ts), where k is a positive constant depending on the surface area and nature of the body, T is the body temperature, and Ts is the surrounding temperature.
steps: Place a cup of hot chai on your study table and notice how it cools faster initially when steaming hot, but slows down as it approaches room temperature
This everyday observation is exactly what Newton quantified
Begin by identifying the temperature difference (T - Ts) as the driving force for heat loss
Connect this to the calorimetry principle from node c11_phy_cbse_10_008: the heat lost dQ = ms dT
Equate the rate of heat loss from Newton's law to the rate of temperature change from calorimetry to get the differential equation ms(dT/dt) = -k(T - Ts)
The solution gives an exponential decay of temperature difference with time, which you can verify by plotting ln(T - Ts) versus t.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer like "k has unit W/m²K" reveals confusion with thermal conductivity or heat transfer coefficient; k here is for the entire body, not per unit area.
remember: State Newton's Law of Cooling mathematically and write the SI unit of the proportionality constant k.
Why does Newton's Law of Cooling hold only for small temperature differences? Explain using the physics of heat transfer modes involved.
A copper sphere of mass 0.2 kg and specific heat 385 J/kg·K cools from 80°C to 70°C in 5 minutes in a room at 20°C. Calculate the cooling constant k for this sphere.

cards.title: A thermodynamic system is a specific portion of the universe (a definite…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: A thermodynamic system is a specific portion of the universe (a definite quantity of matter or a region in space) chosen for thermodynamic analysis, separated from the rest of the universe by a real or imaginary boundary. The surroundings comprise everything external to the system that can exchange energy (heat or work) with it. The boundary is the interface across which interactions occur; it may be fixed or movable, conducting (diathermic) or insulating (adiabatic).
steps: Observe a pressure cooker on a stove: the water and steam inside constitute the system, the metal pot is the boundary, and the kitchen air, stove flame, and countertop are the surroundings
Notice that steam cannot escape (closed system) but heat flows through the metal (diathermic boundary)

Now consider a thermos flask: tea inside is the system, the double-walled vacuum is an adiabatic boundary preventing heat flow, and the outer air is surroundings – this approximates an isolated system
Contrast with an open beaker of water: water vapor escapes (mass transfer), making it an open system
To specify the state of the gas in the pressure cooker, we only need macroscopic variables like pressure (P), volume (V), temperature (T), and moles (n) – not the motion of individual molecules
This macroscopic description is the essence of thermodynamics.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., calling the vacuum layer diathermic) reveals confusion between heat conduction and insulation, or inability to identify the boundary material's thermal property.
