cards.title: The Zeroth Law of Thermodynamics states that if two thermodynamic systems are…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: The Zeroth Law of Thermodynamics states that if two thermodynamic systems are each in thermal equilibrium with a third system separately, then they are in thermal equilibrium with each other. Thermal equilibrium between two systems occurs when they are connected by a diathermic (heat-conducting) wall and no net energy transfer as heat takes place between them, which implies they have the same temperature. Temperature is thus the macroscopic thermodynamic variable that determines whether systems are in thermal equilibrium.
steps: Begin with a familiar observation: when you place a cold steel spoon into a hot cup of chai, the spoon warms up and the chai cools slightly until both feel the same "hotness" to your lips – they have reached thermal…
Ask: what physical quantity becomes equal? Guide students to recognize it is temperature, not heat content
Then introduce two gas-filled containers separated by an adiabatic wall (thermos flask wall) – their pressures and volumes can be arbitrary and remain unchanged
Replace the wall with a diathermic one (copper sheet) – pressures and volumes change spontaneously until they stop
at that point the systems share a common temperature
Finally, present the three-system thought experiment (A, B, C) to deduce the transitive Zeroth Law and establish temperature as the state variable that tags equilibrium classes.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., citing the First Law or saying "heat becomes equal") reveals confusion between energy conservation and the logical foundation of temperature.
remember: State the Zeroth Law of Thermodynamics in your own words and name the thermodynamic variable it allows us to define.

cards.title: The First Law of Thermodynamics states that the heat energy (ΔQ) supplied to a…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: The First Law of Thermodynamics states that the heat energy (ΔQ) supplied to a thermodynamic system equals the sum of the increase in its internal energy (ΔU) and the work done by the system on its surroundings (ΔW), expressed as ΔQ = ΔU + ΔW. Internal energy (U) is the total microscopic energy of a system — the sum of kinetic and potential energies of its constituent molecules relative to the centre-of-mass frame — measured in joules (J); it is a state variable depending only on the thermodynamic state (P, V, T), not on the path taken to reach that state.
steps: Imagine a pressure cooker on a stove: the flame supplies heat (ΔQ), the steam inside pushes the weighted lid upward doing work (ΔW), and the remaining energy raises the temperature and pressure of the steam — that…
Begin by identifying the system (the steam) and surroundings (flame, lid, atmosphere)
Recall from Class 9 (Work-Energy Theorem) that energy is conserved
here we extend it to include microscopic thermal energy
Measure initial and final states (P, V, T) to find ΔU using the First Law
The key principle: energy transferred as heat and work changes the internal energy, a state function.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., ΔQ = ΔU – ΔW or missing sign convention) reveals confusion between the physics sign convention (system-centric) and the chemistry convention (surroundings-centric), or failure to recognise that both heat and work are energy in transit…
remember: State the First Law of Thermodynamics in equation form, define each symbol with its SI unit, and state the sign convention for heat supplied to the system and work done by the….

cards.title: Work done in an isothermal process is the energy transferred by an ideal gas as…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Work done in an isothermal process is the energy transferred by an ideal gas as work when it expands or compresses at constant temperature, calculated by integrating pressure with respect to volume under the condition that the product of pressure and volume remains constant (Boyle's law). For an ideal gas undergoing a quasi-static isothermal change from volume V₁ to V₂ at temperature T, the work done by the gas is W = μRT ln(V₂/V₁), where μ is the number of moles and R is the universal gas constant (8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹). The SI unit of work is joule (J).
steps: Imagine a bicycle pump with its nozzle blocked, placed in a bucket of water at room temperature
If you push the piston slowly, the air inside compresses but its temperature stays constant because heat flows into the water
This is a quasi-static isothermal compression
To analyze it, first recall that for an ideal gas at constant temperature, pressure varies inversely with volume (Boyle's law: PV = constant)
The work done in a small volume change dV is dW = P dV
Substitute P = μRT/V from the ideal gas equation, then integrate from V₁ to V₂
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., using Celsius for T, or omitting the logarithm) reveals confusion between isothermal and isobaric work formulas or misunderstanding that temperature must be in absolute scale for the ideal gas equation.
remember: State the formula for work done by an ideal gas in a quasi-static isothermal process and give the SI unit of each variable in the formula.

cards.title: Work done in an adiabatic process is the energy transferred by a gas when it…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Work done in an adiabatic process is the energy transferred by a gas when it expands or compresses without any heat exchange with its surroundings (Q = 0). For a quasi-static adiabatic process of an ideal gas, the work done by the gas is given by \( W = \frac{P_1V_1 - P_2V_2}{\gamma - 1} = \frac{\mu R (T_1 - T_2)}{\gamma - 1} \), where \( \gamma = C_p/C_v \) is the adiabatic index. The SI unit of work is the joule (J). A positive value indicates work done by the gas (expansion), while a negative value indicates work done on the gas (compression).
steps: Observe a bicycle pump: when you rapidly compress air by pushing the piston down, the pump barrel becomes noticeably warm
This heating occurs because work is done on the gas adiabatically (no time for heat to escape), increasing its internal energy and temperature
Conversely, when you release the valve on a pressurized tyre, the escaping air feels cold because the gas does work on the surroundings adiabatically, decreasing its internal energy
Connect this to the First Law (c11_phy_cbse_11_003): since Q = 0, ΔU = -W
For an ideal gas, ΔU = nC_vΔT, so the work done is directly linked to the temperature change
The key step is recognizing that for adiabatic processes, pressure and volume are related by PV^γ = constant, which allows us to integrate PdV to find the work done.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., stating Q = constant or using the isothermal formula W = nRT ln(V2/V1)) reveals confusion between adiabatic and isothermal processes, or a misunderstanding that "adiabatic" means constant temperature.
remember: State the condition for a process to be adiabatic and write the expression for work done by an ideal gas in a quasi-static adiabatic process in terms of initial and final….

cards.title: Molar specific heat capacity at constant volume (Cᵥ) is the amount of heat…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Molar specific heat capacity at constant volume (Cᵥ) is the amount of heat required to raise the temperature of one mole of a gas by 1 K while keeping its volume constant. Molar specific heat capacity at constant pressure (Cₚ) is the amount of heat required to raise the temperature of one mole of a gas by 1 K while keeping its pressure constant. Both are measured in J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹. For an ideal gas, Cₚ > Cᵥ because at constant pressure, part of the supplied heat is used to do expansion work against the external pressure.
steps: Imagine heating a gas in a rigid steel cylinder (like an LPG cylinder) versus heating it in a piston-cylinder arrangement (like a bicycle pump with the outlet blocked)
In the rigid cylinder, the volume cannot change, so all heat supplied goes into increasing internal energy
In the piston-cylinder, the gas expands, pushing the piston outward — some heat energy is converted into mechanical work
This everyday observation shows why more heat is needed per degree rise at constant pressure than at constant volume
We begin by recalling the First Law (ΔQ = ΔU + ΔW) and the ideal gas equation (PV = μRT)
For a constant volume process, ΔW = 0, so ΔQ = ΔU
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹) reveals confusion between specific heat capacity (per unit mass) and molar specific heat capacity (per mole). Missing the subscript v or p indicates the student does not grasp that the path/process matters for heat capacity.
remember: State the SI units of molar specific heat capacity at constant volume (Cᵥ) and constant pressure….
Explain why Cₚ is greater than Cᵥ for any ideal gas, using the First Law of Thermodynamics. Do not just state the formula Cₚ − Cᵥ = R.
Two moles of an ideal gas are heated at constant volume from 300 K to 340 K. The heat supplied is measured as 2500 J. Calculate Cᵥ and Cₚ for this gas. (R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹).

cards.title: Mayer's formula states that for an ideal gas…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Mayer's formula states that for an ideal gas, the difference between the molar specific heat capacity at constant pressure (Cp) and the molar specific heat capacity at constant volume (Cv) is equal to the universal gas constant R. Mathematically, Cp – Cv = R, where Cp and Cv are in J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ and R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹. This relation arises because at constant pressure, part of the heat supplied is used to do work of expansion, whereas at constant volume, all heat goes into increasing internal energy.
steps: Imagine a pressure cooker on a stove: when heated, the steam inside builds pressure and lifts the weight (does work), whereas if the same steam were in a rigid sealed container, all heat would only raise temperature and…
Start by recalling the first law: ΔQ = ΔU + ΔW
For one mole of ideal gas at constant volume, ΔW = 0 so Cv = (ΔQ/ΔT)_v = (ΔU/ΔT)
At constant pressure, ΔW = PΔV = RΔT (from PV = RT), so Cp = (ΔQ/ΔT)_p = (ΔU/ΔT) + R
Subtracting gives Cp – Cv = R
Emphasize that ΔU/ΔT is the same in both cases because internal energy of an ideal gas depends only on temperature.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., Cp – Cv = 0 or Cp/Cv = R) reveals confusion between the difference and ratio of specific heats, or ignorance that R has the same units as specific heat capacities.
remember: State Mayer's formula for an ideal gas and give the SI units of each term.
Explain why Cp is greater than Cv for an ideal gas, using the first law of thermodynamics.
One mole of an ideal gas has Cv = 20.8 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹. Calculate Cp and the ratio γ = Cp/Cv.

cards.title: An isothermal process is a thermodynamic process in which the temperature of…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: An isothermal process is a thermodynamic process in which the temperature of the system remains constant (ΔT = 0) throughout, achieved by allowing heat exchange with a thermal reservoir so that ΔU = 0 for an ideal gas and Q = W. An adiabatic process is a thermodynamic process in which no heat is exchanged between the system and its surroundings (Q = 0), so the change in internal energy is entirely due to work done (ΔU = -W), resulting in a temperature change. The comparison focuses on how pressure, volume, and temperature relate (PV = constant vs. PV^γ = constant), the slope of their P-V curves (adiabatic steeper by factor γ), and the direction of energy flow.
steps: Observe a bicycle pump: when you compress air rapidly by pushing the piston quickly, the pump barrel becomes noticeably warm — this is an adiabatic compression because there is no time for heat to escape
Now imagine the same compression done extremely slowly while the pump is immersed in a large water bath at constant temperature
the water absorbs any heat generated, keeping the gas temperature constant — this is isothermal compression
Start by recalling the First Law (ΔQ = ΔU + ΔW) and the ideal gas internal energy dependence on temperature only (ΔU = nC_vΔT)
For isothermal, set ΔT=0 → ΔU=0 → Q=W
For adiabatic, set Q=0 → ΔU = -W
cards.misconception: A wrong answer like "isothermal means Q=0" reveals confusion between "no temperature change" and "no heat exchange" — the student is mixing up the two processes.
remember: State the defining thermodynamic condition for an isothermal process and an adiabatic process in terms of heat exchange (Q) and temperature change….

cards.title: The Second Law of Thermodynamics introduces a fundamental directionality to…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: The Second Law of Thermodynamics introduces a fundamental directionality to natural processes that the First Law (energy conservation) alone cannot explain. It is stated in two equivalent classical forms: the Kelvin-Planck statement asserts that no cyclic process can have the sole effect of completely converting heat absorbed from a single thermal reservoir into an equivalent amount of work; the Clausius statement asserts that no cyclic process can have the sole effect of transferring heat from a colder body to a hotter body without external work being performed on the system. Both statements imply that the efficiency of any heat engine must be strictly less than 1 (η < 1) and the coefficient of performance of any refrigerator must be finite (α < ∞).
steps: Imagine a hot cup of chai left on a table in a Delhi winter: it spontaneously cools down, transferring heat to the cooler air
The First Law allows the reverse – the chai spontaneously heating up by absorbing heat from the cold air – because energy would be conserved
Yet we never observe this
To understand why, we first recall the First Law (c11_phy_cbse_11_003): ΔQ = ΔU + ΔW
A heat engine takes heat Q₁ from a hot reservoir, does work W, and rejects heat Q₂ to a cold reservoir
The Kelvin-Planck statement says Q₂ can never be zero in a cyclic process
cards.misconception: A wrong answer stating η = 1 reveals the student thinks the First Law alone governs energy conversion, ignoring the directional constraint of the Second…
remember: State the Kelvin-Planck statement of the Second Law of….
A student claims: "The First Law says energy is conserved, so if I build a frictionless engine that absorbs 1000 J from a hot reservoir and does exactly 1000 J of work, I haven't….

cards.title: A thermodynamic process is reversible if it can be reversed such that both the…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: A thermodynamic process is reversible if it can be reversed such that both the system and the surroundings return to their original states with no net change anywhere else in the universe; it is irreversible if it cannot be reversed without leaving a net change in the universe. Reversibility requires the process to be quasi-static (infinitesimally slow, maintaining equilibrium at every stage) and free from dissipative effects like friction, viscosity, or unrestrained expansion.
steps: Observe a gas leaking from a punctured LPG cylinder in a kitchen – the gas spreads irreversibly throughout the room and never spontaneously returns to the cylinder
Ask: "What would need to happen for this to reverse?" Guide students to see that reversal would require external work (a compressor) and would heat the surroundings, leaving a net change
Contrast with an idealised frictionless piston compressing gas infinitely slowly: at each step, an infinitesimal pressure difference drives the change, and the process can be retraced exactly
Connect to prior nodes: thermal equilibrium (c11_phy_cbse_11_002) defines the quasi-static condition
First Law (c11_phy_cbse_11_003) shows energy conservation
Second Law (c11_phy_cbse_11_009) forbids complete heat-to-work conversion, making reversibility the theoretical limit for maximum efficiency.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer listing only "slow process" or only "no friction" reveals the student misses that both conditions must hold simultaneously – a slow process with friction is irreversible, and a fast frictionless process passes through non-equilibrium states.
remember: State the two necessary and sufficient conditions for a thermodynamic process to be reversible.
Why is the free expansion of a gas into vacuum (Joule expansion) irreversible even though no friction is involved.

cards.title: The Carnot engine is an idealized reversible heat engine operating between two…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: The Carnot engine is an idealized reversible heat engine operating between two thermal reservoirs at temperatures T₁ (source) and T₂ (sink) that achieves the maximum possible efficiency for given reservoir temperatures. Its efficiency is given by η = 1 - T₂/T₁, where temperatures must be in Kelvin, and is independent of the working substance.
steps: Imagine a pressure cooker on a stove - steam pushes the lid up (work) but some heat escapes
Now ask: what is the absolute best fraction of heat we could convert to work if we had perfect insulation and no…
Then isothermal compression rejects heat Q₂ at T₂, and adiabatic compression returns to T₁
The key insight: for reversible adiabats, TV^(γ-1) = constant, which links volume ratios to temperature ratios
This makes the ln(V₂/V₁) terms cancel, leaving only temperatures.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer using Celsius reveals the student doesn't understand thermodynamic temperature must be absolute; stating "real engines can be more efficient" reveals misunderstanding of the Second Law's limitation.
remember: State the efficiency formula for a Carnot engine and specify the temperature unit….

cards.title: The Coefficient of Performance (COP) of a refrigerator, denoted by α (alpha)…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: The Coefficient of Performance (COP) of a refrigerator, denoted by α (alpha), is a dimensionless measure of its effectiveness defined as the ratio of heat extracted from the cold reservoir (Q₂) to the work input (W) required to achieve this extraction: α = Q₂/W. For a Carnot (reversible) refrigerator operating between a cold reservoir at temperature T₂ and a hot reservoir at temperature T₁ (T₁ > T₂), the maximum possible COP is given by α_Carnot = T₂/(T₁ - T₂), where temperatures must be in Kelvin. This quantifies how many joules of heat are removed from the cold space per joule of work supplied.
steps: Observe a household refrigerator: it keeps the inside cold (≈ 4°C) while the kitchen is warm (≈ 30°C), and its compressor motor consumes electricity
This is heat flowing from cold to hot, which the Clausius statement says cannot happen without external work
Begin by identifying the three energy transfers: Q₂ (heat removed from inside), W (work done by compressor), and Q₁ (heat rejected to kitchen)
Apply the First Law to the cyclic device: Q₁ = Q₂ + W
The "performance" we want is cooling effect per unit cost, so define α = Q₂/W
For an ideal reversible (Carnot) refrigerator, use the universal relation Q₁/T₁ = Q₂/T₂ to eliminate Q₁ and derive α = T₂/(T₁ - T₂)
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., α = W/Q₂ or stating units as J) reveals confusion between refrigerator COP and heat engine efficiency, or a misunderstanding that COP is a ratio of two energies and thus unitless.
remember: Define the Coefficient of Performance (COP) of a refrigerator. State its formula in terms of heat extracted (Q₂) and work done (W), and give its SI unit.
A student claims: "The COP of a refrigerator is always less than 1 because efficiency can never exceed 100%." Explain why this reasoning is incorrect, using the First Law and the….

cards.title: The kinetic theory of gases is a theoretical model based on seven fundamental…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: The kinetic theory of gases is a theoretical model based on seven fundamental postulates (assumptions) that describe an ideal gas as a large collection of point-like molecules in continuous, random motion, obeying Newton's laws, with perfectly elastic collisions and negligible intermolecular forces except during instantaneous collisions.
steps: Imagine you inflate a balloon and squeeze it — you feel a uniform resistance from all sides
Now recall from Class 9 that matter is made of particles (c9_physics_ch1_2: Model Building)
If the balloon contains gas, what are those particles doing? Begin by observing that gases fill their container completely and exert pressure on walls
Ask: what microscopic behaviour explains this macroscopic pressure? The first step is to assume molecules exist and move randomly — this connects to Brownian motion evidence
Next, realise that if molecules had large volume or strong attraction, the gas would not be so compressible
So we assume point masses with no forces
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., missing "random motion" or confusing "elastic" with "inelastic") reveals the student has memorised keywords without understanding the physical role of each assumption in simplifying the derivation of pressure.
remember: State the seven assumptions of the kinetic theory of an ideal gas as per the NCERT textbook.
Why is the assumption that "molecules are point masses with negligible volume" essential for deriving the ideal gas….

cards.title: Pressure of an ideal gas, derived from kinetic theory…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Pressure of an ideal gas, derived from kinetic theory, is the macroscopic force per unit area exerted by gas molecules on the container walls due to elastic collisions, given by P = (1/3) n m ⟨v²⟩ = (1/3) ρ v_rms², where n is number density (molecules/m³), m is molecular mass (kg), ⟨v²⟩ is mean square speed (m²/s²), ρ = nm is mass density (kg/m³), and v_rms = √⟨v²⟩ is root mean square speed (m/s). This formula holds for a gas satisfying kinetic theory assumptions: large number of molecules in random motion, negligible volume compared to container, elastic collisions, and no intermolecular forces except during collisions.
steps: Imagine a pressure cooker whistle rattling — steam molecules bombard the lid, creating upward force
This is pressure from molecular collisions
In Class 9 you learned that force equals rate of change of momentum (F = Δp/Δt)
Now consider a single molecule in a cubical box hitting a wall: its x-velocity reverses, so Δpₓ = 2mvₓ
How many such hits occur per second? Only molecules within distance vₓΔt of the wall, and only half move toward it
Multiply momentum transfer per hit by hit rate, sum over all molecules, and use the fact that motion is equally likely in x, y, z directions (isotropy) to replace ⟨vₓ²⟩ with ⅓⟨v²⟩
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., missing 1/3, confusing n with total number N, or omitting units) reveals the student has memorized the formula without understanding the vector decomposition or the distinction between number density and total molecule count.
remember: Write the kinetic theory formula for pressure of an ideal gas, defining each symbol with its SI….

cards.title: The kinetic interpretation of temperature states that the absolute temperature…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: The kinetic interpretation of temperature states that the absolute temperature (T) of an ideal gas is a direct measure of the average translational kinetic energy per molecule, given by (1/2)m⟨v²⟩ = (3/2)k_BT, where m is the molecular mass, ⟨v²⟩ is the mean square speed, and k_B = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J/K is the Boltzmann constant. This establishes temperature as a purely microscopic statistical quantity independent of the gas's chemical nature, pressure, or volume.
steps: Observe a pressure cooker whistle: as water boils, steam molecules move faster, hitting the lid more frequently and forcefully, raising pressure until the whistle lifts
This everyday phenomenon connects macroscopic pressure-temperature behaviour to microscopic molecular motion
Begin by recalling the pressure derivation from the previous node: P = (1/3)nm⟨v²⟩
Combine this with the ideal gas law PV = Nk_BT, which you learned in Class 9 chemistry (mole concept)
Equate the two expressions for PV, cancel common terms, and isolate the kinetic energy term
The key insight emerges: (1/2)m⟨v²⟩ = (3/2)k_BT
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., writing v_rms instead of ⟨v²⟩, or using R instead of k_B) reveals confusion between molecular and molar quantities, or between speed and mean square speed.
remember: State the kinetic interpretation of temperature equation and identify the physical meaning of each symbol with its SI unit.

cards.title: Root mean square (rms) speed is the square root of the mean of the squares of…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Root mean square (rms) speed is the square root of the mean of the squares of the speeds of all molecules in a gas sample. It is a measure of the typical molecular speed in a gas and is given by \(v_{\text{rms}} = \sqrt{\frac{3k_B T}{m}} = \sqrt{\frac{3RT}{M}}\), where \(k_B\) is Boltzmann constant, \(T\) is absolute temperature (K), \(m\) is mass of one molecule (kg), \(R\) is universal gas constant, and \(M\) is molar mass (kg/mol). SI unit: m/s.
steps: Observe a pressure cooker whistle: steam escapes at high speed, creating sound
The speed of those steam molecules is related to the temperature inside
Begin by recalling the kinetic theory pressure formula \(P = \frac{1}{3} n m \overline{v^2}\) from the previous node (c11_phy_cbse_12_002)
Combine it with the ideal gas law \(PV = nRT\) (or \(PV = N k_B T\)) to eliminate pressure and volume
The key step is recognizing that \(\overline{v^2}\) is the mean square speed, so its square root is \(v_{\text{rms}}\)
Emphasize that temperature MUST be in Kelvin and molar mass in kg/mol for SI consistency
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., using \(M\) in g/mol without conversion, or using Celsius) reveals the student does not track SI unit consistency in the formula.
remember: Write the formula for root mean square speed of gas molecules in terms of universal gas constant \(R\), absolute temperature \(T\), and molar mass….
Two gases, hydrogen (molar mass 2 g/mol) and oxygen (32 g/mol), are at the same….
Calculate the rms speed of nitrogen gas (\(M = 28\ \text{g/mol}\)) at \(27^\circ\text{C}\). Use \(R = 8.31\ \text{J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}\).

cards.title: Degrees of freedom of a gas molecule is the number of independent parameters…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Degrees of freedom of a gas molecule is the number of independent parameters (translational, rotational, vibrational) needed to specify its microscopic state. The Law of Equipartition of Energy states that in thermal equilibrium at absolute temperature T, each quadratic degree of freedom contributes an average energy of (1/2)k_BT per molecule, where k_B is the Boltzmann constant (1.38 × 10⁻²³ J/K).
steps: Imagine a ceiling fan rotating in your room — its blades have kinetic energy from rotation
Now think of an oxygen molecule: it translates through the room, rotates like a tiny dumbbell, and its two atoms vibrate toward and away from each other like a spring
Each independent motion is a "degree of freedom." Start by identifying how many coordinates are needed to locate a molecule in space (3 for translation)
Then ask: can it rotate? A diatomic molecule has 2 independent axes of rotation (not 3, because rotation along the bond has negligible moment of inertia)
Finally, consider vibration: it adds both kinetic and potential energy terms, so it counts as 2 degrees of freedom
The equipartition theorem then assigns (1/2)k_BT to each quadratic term, letting us predict specific heats.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., stating k_BT or (3/2)k_BT) reveals confusion between total translational energy and energy per degree of freedom, or misunderstanding that the theorem applies per quadratic term, not per molecule overall.
remember: State the law of equipartition of energy and write the average energy per molecule for a single quadratic degree of freedom at temperature T.
A diatomic gas molecule is modeled as a rigid rotator at room….

cards.title: Specific heat capacity of a gas is the amount of heat required to raise the…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Specific heat capacity of a gas is the amount of heat required to raise the temperature of one mole of the gas by one kelvin, measured under specified conditions of constant volume (Cv) or constant pressure (Cp). For an ideal gas, the molar specific heat at constant volume is Cv = (f/2)R and at constant pressure is Cp = Cv + R = (f/2 + 1)R, where f is the number of active degrees of freedom per molecule and R = 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ is the universal gas constant. The ratio γ = Cp/Cv = (f+2)/f characterises the gas's thermodynamic behaviour.
steps: Observe a pressure cooker whistle: steam (polyatomic) escapes violently while the metal body (solid) heats slowly
Why does steam carry so much more energy per degree than the metal? Students already know from c11_phy_cbse_12_005 that each quadratic energy term stores ½kBT

Begin by listing the independent ways a molecule can store energy: three translations for all gases, two rotations for a linear diatomic molecule, and for a vibrating bond, both kinetic and potential energy quadratics
Count these "slots" (degrees of freedom), multiply by ½R per mole per slot, and add R for the work done during expansion at constant pressure
This directly yields Cv, Cp, and γ without memorisation.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., Cv = 3R) reveals the student is counting degrees of freedom incorrectly or confusing per-molecule (½kB) with per-mole (½R) energy contributions.
remember: State the molar specific heat at constant volume (Cv) and constant pressure (Cp) for a monoatomic ideal gas, and give the value of γ = Cp/Cv. Include SI units.
A diatomic gas like oxygen has two rotational degrees of freedom at room….
Calculate the molar specific heat at constant volume (Cv) and the ratio γ for a rigid diatomic….

cards.title: Mean free path is the average distance traveled by a gas molecule between two…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Mean free path is the average distance traveled by a gas molecule between two successive collisions with other molecules. It is a statistical quantity representing the mean of the free paths of all molecules in a gas at equilibrium. The SI unit is metre (m). For an ideal gas of rigid spherical molecules of diameter \(d\) and number density \(n\), the mean free path \(\lambda\) is given by \(\lambda = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2} \pi d^2 n}\).
steps: Observe that when a gas cylinder leaks in a kitchen, the smell takes minutes to reach the other corner even though molecules move at ~500 m/s
This is because molecules collide frequently, deflecting their paths
Imagine a single molecule moving through a crowd of stationary molecules: it sweeps a cylindrical volume \(\pi d^2 \langle v \rangle \Delta t\) in time \(\Delta t\)
Any molecule whose centre lies in this cylinder will collide
The number of collisions is \(n \pi d^2 \langle v \rangle \Delta t\), giving collision frequency \(n \pi d^2 \langle v \rangle\)
The average distance between collisions is \(\langle v \rangle\) divided by this frequency, yielding \(\lambda = 1/(\pi d^2 n)\)
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., omitting \(\sqrt{2}\) or using \(r\) instead of \(d\)) reveals confusion between the simplified derivation (stationary targets) and the exact result (moving targets), or confusion between radius and diameter.
remember: State the definition of mean free path and write its exact formula in terms of molecular diameter \(d\) and number density \(n\). What is its SI unit.
In the exact derivation of mean free path, a factor of \(1/\sqrt{2}\) appears compared to the simplified….
Calculate the mean free path of nitrogen molecules at STP (0°C, 1 atm). Given: molecular diameter of N₂ = 3.7 Å, molar volume at STP = 22.4 L. Show all steps with units.

cards.title: Avogadro's number (N_A) is the number of constituent particles (atoms or…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Avogadro's number (N_A) is the number of constituent particles (atoms or molecules) in one mole of a substance, defined exactly as 6.02214076 × 10²³ mol⁻¹. The ideal gas law states that for an ideal gas, the product of pressure (P) and volume (V) is directly proportional to the number of moles (μ) and the absolute temperature (T): PV = μRT, where R = 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ is the universal gas constant. Equivalently, PV = N k_B T, where N is the total number of molecules and k_B = R/N_A = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹ is the Boltzmann constant.
steps: Observe a pressure cooker whistle: steam escapes at high pressure and temperature
Ask: "If we trap a fixed amount of gas in a container, how do P, V, and T relate?" Start with Boyle's law (P ∝ 1/V at constant T) and Charles's law (V ∝ T at constant P) from Class 11 Thermodynamics
Combine them to get PV ∝ T for a fixed gas sample
Introduce the proportionality constant as μR, where μ is the amount of substance in moles
Define one mole using carbon-12: the amount containing as many entities as atoms in 12 g of ¹²C
Avogadro's number is that count
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., giving R = 0.0821 L atm mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ without converting to SI, or confusing N_A with k_B) reveals the student has not internalized the SI unit system or the distinction between molar and molecular forms.
remember: State Avogadro's hypothesis and write the ideal gas equation in terms of (i) number of moles μ and (ii) number of molecules N. Give the SI units and values of R and k_B.
Explain why the ideal gas law fails at high pressures and low temperatures. Use the concepts of molecular volume and intermolecular forces.
A 10.0 L cylinder contains oxygen gas at 27°C and 150 atm gauge….

cards.title: Maxwell's Speed Distribution Law describes the statistical distribution of…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Maxwell's Speed Distribution Law describes the statistical distribution of molecular speeds in an ideal gas at thermal equilibrium, giving the fraction of molecules having speeds between v and v+dv as f(v)dv = 4π (m/2πk_BT)^{3/2} v^2 e^{-mv^2/2k_BT} dv, where m is the molecular mass (kg), k_B is the Boltzmann constant (1.38×10^{-23} J/K), and T is the absolute temperature (K). The distribution is asymmetric, peaking at the most probable speed v_p = √(2k_BT/m), with mean speed v_avg = √(8k_BT/πm) and root-mean-square speed v_rms = √(3k_BT/m), satisfying v_p < v_avg < v_rms.
steps: Imagine releasing a drop of perfume in one corner of a classroom – the scent doesn't reach everyone at once because air molecules move at vastly different speeds, not a single uniform speed
In Class 9 you learned that gas pressure arises from molecular collisions, but we treated all molecules as having the same rms speed
Now we ask: what is the actual spread of speeds? Start by plotting a histogram of molecular speeds from a simulation – you'll see a skewed bell curve
The peak gives the most probable speed v_p, the area under the curve is total molecules, and the average speed v_avg is the first moment
Connect this to the kinetic interpretation of temperature (c11_phy_cbse_12_003): since average kinetic energy is fixed by T, lighter molecules must have a broader, right-shifted distribution
The key formula f(v) = 4π (m/2πk_BT)^{3/2} v^2 e^{-mv^2/2k_BT} emerges from maximizing entropy subject to energy constraints.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., omitting the v^2 factor or the normalization constant) reveals the student memorizes the exponential but forgets the phase-space volume factor v^2 that makes low speeds less probable than the exponential alone suggests.
remember: State the Maxwell-Boltzmann speed distribution function f(v) for an ideal gas, defining every symbol with its SI unit. What is the physical meaning of f(v)dv.
Explain why the most probable speed v_p is less than the average speed v_avg, which in turn is less than the rms speed v_rms, using the shape of the Maxwell-Boltzmann curve.
Calculate the most probable speed, average speed, and rms speed of nitrogen molecules (M = 28.0 g/mol) at 300 K. Use R = 8.31 J/mol·K and N_A = 6.022×10^{23} mol^{-1}.

cards.title: Periodic motion is a motion that repeats itself identically after a fixed…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Periodic motion is a motion that repeats itself identically after a fixed interval of time called the period (T). Oscillatory motion is a special type of periodic motion where a particle moves to and fro about a stable equilibrium position under the action of a restoring force. The frequency (ν) is the reciprocal of the period (ν = 1/T) measured in hertz (Hz). Displacement in oscillations refers to the change with time of any physical quantity (position, angle, voltage, pressure) from its equilibrium value and can be represented by a sinusoidal function of time.
steps: Observe a ceiling fan rotating at constant speed — its motion repeats but the blade does not move to and fro about a fixed point
it is periodic but not oscillatory
Now observe a swing in a playground: the child moves back and forth about the lowest point (equilibrium)
Use a stopwatch to measure the time for 10 complete to-and-fro motions of the swing
divide by 10 to get the period T
Recall from Class 7 (c7_physics_ch04_002) that the pendulum's period depends on length
cards.misconception: A wrong answer reveals the misconception that all periodic motions are oscillatory.
remember: A student claims that the motion of the Earth around the Sun is oscillatory because it repeats every….
The displacement of a particle in an oscillatory system is given by x(t) = 0.05 cos(10πt) where x is in meters and t in….
A quartz crystal in a digital watch vibrates with a frequency of 32,768 Hz. Calculate its period of vibration in microseconds (μs). Show unit conversion steps.

cards.title: Simple Harmonic Motion (SHM) is a special type of periodic oscillatory motion…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Simple Harmonic Motion (SHM) is a special type of periodic oscillatory motion where the displacement of a particle from its equilibrium position varies sinusoidally with time, given by \( x(t) = A \cos(\omega t + \phi) \) or equivalently \( x(t) = A \sin(\omega t + \phi) \), where \( A \) is the amplitude (maximum displacement, unit: metre), \( \omega \) is the angular frequency (unit: rad/s), and \( \phi \) is the phase constant (unit: radian). Equivalently, SHM is defined by the restoring force law \( F = -kx \) (or acceleration \( a = -\omega^2 x \)), where the force is directly proportional to the displacement and always directed towards the mean position.
steps: Observe a swinging pendulum in a grandfather clock or a mass oscillating on a spring in a school laboratory
Notice that the motion repeats after a fixed time and the object moves symmetrically about a central point
Ask: "What mathematical function describes this to-and-fro motion?" Start by measuring displacement from the centre at regular time intervals
Plot displacement vs time – the graph resembles a sine/cosine wave
Connect this to the periodic functions studied in Class 11 Mathematics (trigonometric functions)
Introduce the defining equation \( x = A \cos(\omega t + \phi) \) and explain each parameter
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., writing \( x = A \sin(\omega t) \) without phase, or confusing \( \omega \) with frequency \( \nu \)) reveals the student has not internalised the general form with phase constant or the distinction between angular frequency and ordinary…
remember: State the defining equation for displacement in SHM and name each symbol with its SI unit.
A particle moves according to \( x(t) = 5 \cos(2t) + 3 \sin(2t) \). Is this SHM? Explain why or why not without solving for a single sinusoidal function.
The displacement of a particle is given by \( x(t) = 0.04 \cos(10\pi t + \pi/3) \) metre. Calculate the amplitude, period, frequency, and phase constant. Show unit analysis.

cards.title: In Simple Harmonic Motion (SHM)…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: In Simple Harmonic Motion (SHM), displacement x(t) = A cos(ωt + φ) describes the position of a particle relative to its equilibrium position. Velocity is the time derivative v(t) = dx/dt = –ωA sin(ωt + φ), and acceleration is the second derivative a(t) = dv/dt = –ω²A cos(ωt + φ) = –ω²x(t). The SI unit of displacement is metre (m), velocity is m/s, and acceleration is m/s². The negative sign in acceleration indicates it is always directed toward the equilibrium position (restoring).
steps: Observe a ceiling fan blade rotating uniformly — its shadow on the floor moves back and forth in SHM
When the blade is at the extreme left or right, the shadow stops momentarily (v=0) but accelerates maximally toward the centre
When the shadow crosses the centre, it moves fastest (v=max) but acceleration is zero
Start by writing x = A cos(ωt + φ) from the previous node
Differentiate once to get v = –ωA sin(ωt + φ)
Differentiate again to get a = –ω²A cos(ωt + φ) = –ω²x
cards.misconception: A wrong answer like 4 cm/s reveals the student thinks velocity amplitude equals displacement amplitude, ignoring the ω factor. A wrong answer like 8 cm/s reveals the student forgot π in angular…
remember: A particle executes SHM with displacement x = 4 cos(2πt + π/3) where x is in cm and t in s. What is the amplitude of its velocity in cm/s.
In SHM, the acceleration is zero when the particle is at the mean position (x=0), yet the restoring force is also zero….
A body oscillates according to x = 0.05 cos(10πt + π/6) in SI units. Find its displacement, velocity, and acceleration at t = 0.1 s. Show all steps with units.

cards.title: In Simple Harmonic Motion, the total mechanical energy is the sum of kinetic…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: In Simple Harmonic Motion, the total mechanical energy is the sum of kinetic energy (K = ½mv²) and elastic potential energy (U = ½kx²), which remains constant at E = ½kA² for a conservative system. Kinetic energy is maximum at the mean position (x=0) and zero at extremes (x=±A), while potential energy is maximum at extremes and zero at the mean position. Both energies oscillate with frequency twice that of the motion (period T/2).
steps: Observe a swinging pendulum in a grandfather clock or a mass on a spring in a laboratory
Notice how the bob moves fastest at the bottom and momentarily stops at the ends
This speed variation means kinetic energy changes
At the ends, the spring is maximally stretched/compressed or the pendulum is highest—potential energy is maximum there
The total energy stays constant if friction is negligible
We quantify this by writing v = ω√(A²-x²) from the velocity-displacement relation, then substituting into K = ½mv² and U = ½kx²
cards.misconception: A wrong answer like E = kA or E = ½mv²_max reveals the student hasn't connected maximum potential energy (at extremes) to total energy, or confuses maximum kinetic energy with total energy expression in terms of k and A.
remember: State the expression for total mechanical energy of a particle executing SHM with amplitude A and spring constant k. What is its SI unit.
A block on a spring oscillates with amplitude A. At what displacement is the kinetic energy equal to the potential energy? Explain why this happens at that specific position.
A 0.5 kg mass attached to a spring (k = 200 N/m) oscillates with amplitude 0.1 m. Calculate: (a) total energy, (b) maximum speed, (c) kinetic energy at x = 0.05 m.

cards.title: The time period of a simple pendulum is the time taken for the bob to complete…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: The time period of a simple pendulum is the time taken for the bob to complete one full oscillation (from one extreme position to the other and back) under the conditions of small angular displacement (θ < 10°), massless inextensible string, point-mass bob, and negligible air resistance. Its SI unit is second (s). For small oscillations, the motion is simple harmonic with time period T = 2π √(L/g), where L is the effective length from the point of suspension to the centre of mass of the bob, and g is the acceleration due to gravity.
steps: Observe a swing in a playground or a hanging ceiling fan chain pulled slightly sideways and released — it oscillates with a regular period
To begin, identify the forces on the bob: tension along the string and weight mg vertically down
Resolve weight into radial (mg cos θ) and tangential (mg sin θ) components
The tangential component provides the restoring torque about the suspension point
Write the torque equation τ = -mgL sin θ
For small angles, approximate sin θ ≈ θ (in radians), making torque proportional to angular displacement — the condition for angular SHM
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., omitting the 2π, using degrees in the approximation, or stating it works for all amplitudes) reveals the student has memorised the formula without understanding the small-angle approximation or the derivation's origin.
remember: State the formula for the time period of a simple pendulum and write the SI units of each variable. Under what condition is this formula valid.
Why does the time period of a simple pendulum NOT depend on the mass of the bob? Explain using the torque derivation.
A simple pendulum of length 0.80 m is set up in a physics laboratory where g = 9.8….

cards.title: The time period of a spring-mass system is the time taken for the mass to…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: The time period of a spring-mass system is the time taken for the mass to complete one full oscillation about its equilibrium position. For an ideal massless spring of spring constant k (N/m) attached to a block of mass m (kg) on a frictionless horizontal surface, or for a vertical spring-mass system where gravity only shifts the equilibrium position, the period is given by T = 2π√(m/k) seconds. This formula assumes Hooke's law (F = -kx) holds and damping is negligible.
steps: Observe a loaded spring balance in a vegetable market: when the vendor adds tomatoes, the pan oscillates up and down before settling
The time for one complete up-down motion is the period
Begin by identifying the restoring force (Hooke's law: F = -kx) and applying Newton's second law (F = ma) to get a = -(k/m)x
Recognize this matches the SHM condition a = -ω²x, so ω = √(k/m)
The period T = 2π/ω then becomes T = 2π√(m/k)
Connect this to the simple pendulum derivation (c11_phy_cbse_13_005) where ω = √(g/L)
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., T = 2π√(k/m) or missing the 2π) reveals confusion between the spring-mass system and the simple pendulum formula, or a misunderstanding that angular frequency ω = √(k/m) not √(m/k).
remember: State the formula for the time period of a spring-mass system and write the SI unit of each quantity in the formula.
A vertical spring-mass system oscillates with period T on….
A block of mass 0.5 kg is attached to a horizontal spring of spring constant 200 N/m on a frictionless….

cards.title: Damped simple harmonic motion is an oscillatory motion where the amplitude…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Damped simple harmonic motion is an oscillatory motion where the amplitude decreases exponentially with time due to a dissipative damping force (typically viscous, proportional to velocity, F_d = -bv). The displacement is described by x(t) = A₀e^(-bt/2m) cos(ω't + φ) for underdamped systems, where ω' = √(k/m - b²/4m²) is the damped angular frequency, b is the damping constant (SI unit: kg/s or N·s/m), and the total mechanical energy decays as E(t) = E₀e^(-bt/m).
steps: Observe a simple pendulum swinging in air — it gradually slows down and stops, unlike the ideal SHM you studied where it would swing forever
The culprit is air resistance: a force opposing velocity
Now imagine the same pendulum in water — it stops much faster
This "damping" is what we quantify
Start by drawing a free-body diagram of a spring-mass system with an added velocity-dependent force -bv
Apply Newton's second law to get mẍ + bẋ + kx = 0
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., claiming critical damping) reveals the student incorrectly computes the discriminant or confuses the condition b² = 4mk with b = 2√(mk) without squaring properly.
remember: A 0.5 kg mass attached to a spring (k = 200 N/m) oscillates in a fluid providing viscous damping with constant b = 2….
Explain why the motion of a damped oscillator with x(t) = A₀e^(-bt/2m) cos(ω't + φ) is NOT strictly simple harmonic motion, yet the NCERT textbook says it is "approximately so….
A damped oscillator has mass m = 0.2 kg, spring constant k = 80 N/m, and damping constant b = 0.8….

cards.title: Forced oscillations occur when an external periodic force drives a damped…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Forced oscillations occur when an external periodic force drives a damped oscillator at a frequency different from its natural frequency; resonance is the phenomenon where the driving frequency matches the natural frequency of the system, causing the amplitude to reach a maximum limited only by damping. The steady-state amplitude is given by A = (F₀/m) / √[(ω₀² - ω²)² + (2βω)²] where F₀ is the driving force amplitude (N), m is mass (kg), ω₀ is natural angular frequency (rad/s), ω is driving angular frequency (rad/s), and β = b/2m is the damping constant (s⁻¹) with b being the damping coefficient (N·s/m).
steps: Watch a swing in a playground: if you push it at random times, it barely moves, but if you push exactly when it starts moving forward each time, the swing goes higher and higher — this is resonance
In the lab, attach a mass-spring system to a vibration generator and vary the driving frequency while measuring amplitude
you will see a sharp peak at the natural frequency
Connect this to the damped SHM you studied: the external force adds energy each cycle, while damping removes it
The balance between energy input and dissipation determines the steady-state amplitude
The key formula emerges from solving mẍ + bẋ + kx = F₀ cos(ωt) for the particular solution.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer reveals the student ignores the damping shift and confuses natural frequency with resonance frequency — a critical error in engineering applications where damping is significant.
remember: A student writes the resonance condition as ω_d = √(k/m) for a forced damped oscillator. Is this correct? If not, what is the exact resonance frequency for a damped system.
Why does the amplitude not become infinite at resonance in a real system? Explain using energy balance between the driving force and damping force.
A mass-spring system (m = 0.5 kg, k = 200 N/m) has a damping coefficient b = 0.4….

cards.title: In Simple Harmonic Motion described by \( x(t) = A \cos(\omega t + \phi) \)…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: In Simple Harmonic Motion described by \( x(t) = A \cos(\omega t + \phi) \), the phase is the time-dependent argument \( (\omega t + \phi) \) measured in radians that completely specifies the state of the oscillator (displacement and velocity direction) at any instant \( t \). The phase constant (or initial phase) \( \phi \) is the value of the phase at \( t = 0 \); it determines the initial displacement \( x_0 = A \cos \phi \) and initial velocity \( v_0 = -\omega A \sin \phi \). Two SHMs with identical amplitude \( A \) and angular frequency \( \omega \) but different phase constants are said to have a phase difference \( \Delta \phi = \phi_1 - \phi_2 \).
steps: Observe a swing in a playground: when you push a child from rest at the extreme position, the motion starts at maximum displacement
when you give a push at the mean position, it starts with maximum speed
Both are SHM with the same amplitude and frequency but different "starting points." This starting point is quantified by the phase constant \( \phi \)
Begin by writing the general SHM equation \( x = A \cos(\omega t + \phi) \)
At \( t = 0 \), \( x_0 = A \cos \phi \) and \( v_0 = -\omega A \sin \phi \)
Use these two equations to find \( \phi \) given any pair of initial conditions
cards.misconception: A wrong answer like \( \pi/3 \) reveals the student confuses phase constant with instantaneous phase; an answer of \( 120^\circ \) reveals failure to work in radians as required by the argument of trigonometric functions in physics formulas.
remember: A particle executes SHM described by \( x(t) = 5 \cos(4\pi t + \pi/3) \) where \( x \) is in cm and \( t \) in….
Two SHMs are given by \( x_1 = A \cos(\omega t) \) and \( x_2 = A \cos(\omega t + \pi/2)….
A block on a spring executes SHM with amplitude 10 cm and angular frequency \( 2\pi \)….

cards.title: Word problems in SHM applications require translating a physical oscillatory…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Word problems in SHM applications require translating a physical oscillatory system (spring-mass, simple pendulum, floating body, U-tube, etc.) into the standard mathematical model x(t) = A cos(ωt + φ) or its equivalents, identifying parameters (amplitude A, angular frequency ω, phase constant φ) from given conditions, and solving for unknown kinematic or dynamic quantities (displacement, velocity, acceleration, energy, time period) using SHM equations with proper SI units.
steps: Observe a car's suspension system when it hits a speed breaker — the car oscillates up and down before settling
This is a damped spring-mass system, but for small bumps and short times, we approximate it as SHM
To solve such problems, first identify the restoring force: is it a spring (F = –kx), gravity on a pendulum (τ = –mgLθ), or buoyancy (F =…
Third, write the displacement equation using initial conditions (position and velocity at t=0) to find A and φ
Fourth, use x(t), v(t), a(t), or energy equations to answer the specific question
Always convert cm to m, g to kg, and check if the answer is physically plausible (e.g., speed < ωA).
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., writing x = A sin ωt only, or omitting φ, or confusing ω with frequency ν) reveals the student has not internalized the generality of the SHM solution and will struggle with initial-condition problems.
remember: Write the three mathematically equivalent standard forms of the displacement equation for SHM, and state the physical meaning of each symbol with its SI unit.

cards.title: A mechanical wave is classified as transverse if the particles of the medium…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: A mechanical wave is classified as transverse if the particles of the medium oscillate perpendicular to the direction of wave propagation, and longitudinal if the particles oscillate parallel to the direction of wave propagation. In transverse waves, the medium must sustain shear strain (solids, surfaces of liquids); in longitudinal waves, the medium sustains compressive strain (solids, liquids, gases). The SI unit for wave quantities like wavelength (λ) is metre (m), frequency (ν) is hertz (Hz), and wave speed (v) is metre per second (m/s).
steps: Observe a slinky spring on a smooth floor: give one end a sharp sideways jerk — a pulse travels along the slinky while each coil moves left-right (perpendicular to the spring's length)
Now push-pull the same end sharply along the slinky's axis — a compression pulse travels while coils move back-forth (parallel to the length)
The first is a transverse wave
the second is longitudinal
Connect this to Class 9 learning: sound in air is longitudinal (compressions/rarefactions), while waves on a stretched string are transverse
Ask: "Why can't we create a transverse wave in air by shaking a piston sideways?" — this leads to the need for shear rigidity, introducing the core distinction.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer reveals the student is confusing the surface displacement with the actual particle trajectory and has not considered the restoring forces (gravity + surface tension) that produce orbital motion.
remember: A student claims: "Water waves are purely transverse because the water surface moves up and down." State whether this claim is correct or incorrect, and name the actual particle….
Explain why a transverse wave can propagate along a stretched string but not through the air inside a room, even though both are elastic….
A seismic P-wave (primary) travels through the Earth's crust at 6….

cards.title: The speed of a travelling wave is the rate at which a particular phase point…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: The speed of a travelling wave is the rate at which a particular phase point (such as a crest or trough) propagates through a medium, given by v = ω/k = λν = λ/T, where ω is angular frequency, k is angular wave number, λ is wavelength, ν is frequency, and T is period. For mechanical waves, the speed is determined solely by the elastic and inertial properties of the medium: v = √(T/μ) for transverse waves on a stretched string (T = tension, μ = linear mass density), v = √(B/ρ) for longitudinal waves in fluids (B = bulk modulus, ρ = density), and v = √(Y/ρ) for longitudinal waves in solid bars (Y = Young's modulus). SI unit: m/s.
steps: Watch a guitar string being plucked - the disturbance travels along the string at a definite speed
What determines this speed? First, recall from Class 9 that speed = distance/time
For a wave, the distance is one wavelength λ (distance between consecutive crests) and the time is one period T (time for one complete oscillation)
Since the wave travels λ distance in time T, v = λ/T = λν
Now connect this to the wave equation y(x,t) = a sin(kx - ωt): a point of constant phase satisfies kx - ωt = constant, so dx/dt = ω/k
This gives v = ω/k = λν
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., v = k/ω or v = ν/λ) reveals the student has memorised formulas without understanding the phase constancy derivation or the physical meaning of wavelength as distance per cycle and period as time per cycle.
remember: State the three equivalent expressions for the speed of a progressive wave in terms of (i) angular frequency and angular wave number, (ii) wavelength and frequency, (iii)….
A transverse wave travels on a stretched string with speed….
A steel wire of length 1.2 m and mass 6.0 g is stretched under a tension of 150 N. Calculate the speed of a transverse wave on this wire. Show all steps with unit analysis.

cards.title: The speed of sound in air is the rate at which longitudinal pressure…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: The speed of sound in air is the rate at which longitudinal pressure disturbances (compressions and rarefactions) propagate through the medium. Newton's formula assumes isothermal compression/rarefaction giving v = √(P/ρ), while Laplace's correction accounts for adiabatic conditions giving v = √(γP/ρ), where P is the equilibrium pressure (Pa), ρ is the density of air (kg/m³), and γ = Cp/Cv is the ratio of specific heats (dimensionless, 1.4 for diatomic gases like air).
steps: Stand near a railway track and listen to an approaching train's whistle — the sound reaches you through air, not by air flowing from the train to you
Recall from Class 9 that sound is a longitudinal wave of compressions and rarefactions
In Class 11, we quantify its speed using elastic properties: the restoring force comes from pressure changes (bulk modulus B), and inertia comes from density ρ
Begin by writing the general longitudinal wave speed formula v = √(B/ρ) from the previous node (c11_phy_cbse_14_002)
Then examine the thermodynamic process: Newton assumed slow changes (isothermal, B = P), but Laplace recognized sound oscillations are too fast for heat flow (adiabatic, B = γP)
This single conceptual shift — isothermal vs adiabatic — resolves the 15% discrepancy with experiment.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., v = √(γP/ρ) or v = 331 m/s) reveals confusion between Newton's isothermal assumption and Laplace's adiabatic correction, or memorizing the final experimental value without understanding the derivation.

cards.title: The speed of sound in a medium is the rate at which a sound wave propagates…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: The speed of sound in a medium is the rate at which a sound wave propagates through that medium, determined by the medium's elastic (restoring) and inertial (mass density) properties. For an ideal gas, it is given by \( v = \sqrt{\frac{\gamma P}{\rho}} \), where \( \gamma \) is the ratio of specific heats, \( P \) is the pressure, and \( \rho \) is the density; its SI unit is m/s.

cards.title: The principle of superposition of waves states that when two or more waves…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: The principle of superposition of waves states that when two or more waves travel simultaneously through the same region of a medium, the net displacement of any particle of the medium at any instant is the algebraic sum of the displacements produced by each wave individually. This principle holds for linear media where the wave equation is linear, and it applies to both transverse and longitudinal mechanical waves.

To analyze it, we start by writing the displacement equation for each wave separately (using y = a sin(kx - ωt + φ) from c11_phy_cbse_14_003)
Then we add them algebraically at each (x,t)

cards.title: Interference of waves is the phenomenon where two or more coherent waves…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Interference of waves is the phenomenon where two or more coherent waves superpose to form a resultant wave of greater, lower, or the same amplitude. Constructive interference occurs when the phase difference between waves is an even multiple of π (0, 2π, 4π...), causing amplitudes to add and producing maximum intensity. Destructive interference occurs when the phase difference is an odd multiple of π (π, 3π, 5π...), causing amplitudes to cancel and producing minimum or zero intensity.

where crests meet troughs, the surface becomes calm

Apply the trigonometric identity sin A + sin B = 2 sin((A+B)/2) cos((A-B)/2) to find the resultant wave
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., φ = π/2 or claiming constructive interference) reveals the student cannot convert path difference to phase difference using φ = 2πΔx/λ, or does not know that destructive interference requires φ = (2n+1)π.

cards.title: A standing wave (stationary wave) in a string is a wave pattern formed by the…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: A standing wave (stationary wave) in a string is a wave pattern formed by the superposition of two identical progressive waves of same amplitude, frequency, and wavelength traveling in opposite directions along a string fixed at both ends, resulting in fixed points of zero displacement (nodes) and maximum displacement (antinodes) with no net energy transport along the string.

cards.title: Standing waves in pipes are stationary wave patterns formed by the…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Standing waves in pipes are stationary wave patterns formed by the superposition of incident and reflected longitudinal sound waves in an air column, where the boundary conditions (closed end = displacement node/pressure antinode, open end = displacement antinode/pressure node) restrict the allowed wavelengths to discrete values. For a pipe closed at one end, only odd harmonics are present with fundamental frequency \( \nu_1 = \frac{v}{4L} \); for a pipe open at both ends, all harmonics are present with fundamental frequency \( \nu_1 = \frac{v}{2L} \), where \( v \) is the speed of sound in air (m/s) and \( L \) is the pipe length (m).

for an open pipe, a half-wave fits (antinodes at both ends)

cards.title: Beats are the periodic waxing and waning of sound intensity that occurs when…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Beats are the periodic waxing and waning of sound intensity that occurs when two harmonic sound waves of slightly different frequencies (ν₁ and ν₂, with |ν₁ - ν₂| ≈ 5-10 Hz) and comparable amplitudes superpose at a point; the beat frequency ν_beat = |ν₁ - ν₂| equals the absolute difference of the two frequencies, measured in hertz (Hz), and represents the number of intensity maxima (or minima) heard per second.

this is beats

cards.title: The Doppler Effect is the apparent change in frequency (or wavelength) of a…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: The Doppler Effect is the apparent change in frequency (or wavelength) of a wave when there is relative motion between the source of the wave and the observer. For sound waves in a stationary medium, the observed frequency \(f'\) is given by \(f' = f \left(\frac{v \pm v_o}{v \mp v_s}\right)\), where \(f\) is the source frequency, \(v\) is the speed of sound in the medium, \(v_o\) is the speed of the observer (positive if moving toward the source), and \(v_s\) is the speed of the source (positive if moving toward the observer). The upper signs apply when source and observer approach each other; lower signs apply when they recede.
steps: Stand near a railway crossing and listen to a train's horn as it approaches and passes you — the pitch drops sharply at the moment it crosses
This everyday observation is the Doppler Effect

The key insight: for sound, the medium defines a preferred frame, so source motion and observer motion produce different formulas — unlike light where only relative velocity matters.

cards.title: The Doppler effect for sound waves when both the source and observer are in…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: The Doppler effect for sound waves when both the source and observer are in motion relative to the medium is the change in observed frequency due to the relative motion along the line joining them. The observed frequency \( f' \) is given by \( f' = f \frac{v \pm v_o}{v \mp v_s} \), where \( f \) is the source frequency, \( v \) is the speed of sound in the medium, \( v_o \) is the velocity of the observer, and \( v_s \) is the velocity of the source. The upper signs are used when the motion is towards each other (increasing frequency), and lower signs when moving away (decreasing frequency). cards.title: When a travelling wave encounters a boundary, it gets reflected.
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: When a travelling wave encounters a boundary, it gets reflected. At a rigid (fixed) boundary, the reflected wave undergoes a phase change of π rad (180°), meaning a crest reflects as a trough and vice versa. At a free (open) boundary, the reflected wave undergoes no phase change (0 rad), so a crest reflects as a crest. This phase reversal at a rigid boundary arises because the displacement at the boundary must remain zero at all times, which by the principle of superposition requires the incident and reflected waves to be exactly out of phase.

The reflected pulse returns upright
This visible inversion at the fixed end is the π phase change
The key is to realise that at the fixed end, the total displacement must always be zero

cards.title: Politics is the process of collective decision-making and resource allocation…
cards.subject: Political Science
cards.definition: Politics is the process of collective decision-making and resource allocation through which a society negotiates diverse interests, resolves conflicts, and establishes binding rules via authoritative institutions (like government) and participatory mechanisms (like elections, protests, deliberation) to achieve shared goals such as justice, order, and welfare.

cards.title: Politics as the art of government refers to the traditional…
cards.subject: Political Science
cards.definition: Politics as the art of government refers to the traditional, state-centric view of politics as activities associated with governance, law-making, and the exercise of public authority through formal institutions like legislatures, executives, and judiciaries. Politics in everyday life refers to the broader, society-centric understanding of politics as the process of negotiation, conflict resolution, collective decision-making, and power relations that occurs in all social spheres—family, school, workplace, resident welfare associations, and community groups—where scarce resources, status, and values are allocated.

It involves clarifying the meaning of these concepts by analyzing the arguments of political thinkers, both historical and contemporary, and assessing how these values are realized or violated in real-world institutions like government, bureaucracy, schools, and markets.

cards.definition: Political theory is the systematic study of political concepts (freedom, equality, justice, rights) that serves three essential functions: clarity (precise definition of contested concepts), evaluation (critical assessment of arguments, institutions, and policies against normative standards), and guidance (providing principled frameworks for framing public policy and resolving political dilemmas). It transforms vague opinions into reasoned positions by exposing citizens to diverse philosophical traditions and analytical tools.

cards.title: Dharma in Indian political thought refers to the cosmic and moral order that…

cards.title: Eurocentrism in political theory refers to the dominance of European/Western…
cards.subject: Political Science
cards.definition: Eurocentrism in political theory refers to the dominance of European/Western thinkers, concepts, and historical experiences as the universal standard for political thought, marginalizing or ignoring non-Western traditions like Indian, African, or Islamic political philosophy. Abstraction refers to the tendency of political theory to formulate concepts (e.g., justice, liberty, state) at such a high level of generality that they become detached from the lived realities, power structures, and cultural contexts of specific societies, making them difficult to apply to concrete political problems without significant reinterpretation.

cards.title: The Harm Principle, articulated by J.S.
cards.subject: Political Science
cards.definition: The Harm Principle, articulated by J.S. Mill in On Liberty (1859), states that the only justification for interfering with the liberty of an individual, either by state coercion or social pressure, is to prevent harm to others; actions that affect only the individual (self-regarding actions) fall outside the legitimate sphere of external control. cards.definition: Equality of outcomes is a principle of distributive justice which holds that a just society should ensure roughly similar end-results for all citizens in terms of income, wealth, status, and access to essential goods (healthcare, education, housing), regardless of individual talent, effort, or initial advantage. cards.title: Social justice is the principle that a just society must ensure fair…
cards.subject: Political Science
cards.definition: Social justice is the principle that a just society must ensure fair distribution of social goods (resources, opportunities, rights) and burdens (duties, taxes, sacrifices) among all members, balancing three principles: equal treatment for equals, proportional rewards for differential effort/skill, and special provisions for disadvantaged groups to achieve substantive equality of opportunity.

cards.title: John Rawls' "justice as fairness" is a contractarian theory of distributive…
cards.subject: Political Science
cards.definition: John Rawls' "justice as fairness" is a contractarian theory of distributive justice which argues that principles of justice for the basic structure of society must be chosen by rational, mutually disinterested parties situated behind a "veil of ignorance" in an "original position," ensuring impartiality by depriving them of knowledge about their specific social position, natural endowments, and conception of the good.

You'd likely choose rules that protect the worst-off starting position because you might end up there

Start by contrasting this with utilitarianism (greatest happiness for greatest number) which could sacrifice a minority
Then introduce the veil of ignorance as the device that forces impartiality—not by demanding altruism, but by making self-interest align with fairness
Connect to the Class 10 concept of "accommodation of social diversity" (c10_civ_cbse_05_004): Rawls gives a rational, non-sectarian foundation for why a diverse society should protect minorities

cards.title: Rawls' difference principle states that social and economic inequalities are…
cards.subject: Political Science
cards.definition: Rawls' difference principle states that social and economic inequalities are justified only if they benefit the least advantaged members of society; the veil of ignorance is a hypothetical decision-making device where rational individuals choose principles of justice without knowing their own social position, talents, or conception of the good, ensuring impartiality by forcing choice from the perspective of the worst-off.

If you don't know whether you'll be the person who gets the largest slice or the smallest, you will insist on a rule that guarantees the smallest slice is still decent
This is Rawls' insight: fairness emerges not from altruism but from rational self-interest under uncertainty

cards.title: Robert Nozick's entitlement theory of justice holds that a distribution of…
cards.subject: Political Science
cards.definition: Robert Nozick's entitlement theory of justice holds that a distribution of goods is just if it arises from a just starting position via legitimate means: justice in acquisition (initial appropriation of unheld resources), justice in transfer (voluntary exchange, gifts), and justice in rectification (correcting past injustices). It rejects patterned or end-state principles (like Rawls' difference principle) because they require continuous interference with voluntary transactions and violate self-ownership and property rights.

A Rawlsian might ask if the vendor's higher income benefits the least advantaged
a Nozickian asks whether the vendor's earnings came from voluntary customer payments without force or fraud

Start by asking: "If people freely pay ₹50 for a vada pav, does justice require taking part of the vendor's earnings to equalize outcomes?" Connect to the prior node (Rawls' veil of ignorance) by noting that Nozick…

cards.title: The utilitarian approach to justice holds that a just society is one that…
cards.subject: Political Science
cards.definition: The utilitarian approach to justice holds that a just society is one that maximises the overall welfare or happiness of its members, where welfare is understood as the sum total of individual utilities (pleasure, preference satisfaction, or well-being). It evaluates laws, policies, and distributions solely by their consequences for aggregate welfare, requiring that each person's interests count equally in the social calculus.
steps: Imagine the Delhi government must decide whether to spend ₹500 crore on a new super-specialty hospital serving 50,000 critical patients annually or on upgrading 200 primary health centres serving 2 million routine…

A utilitarian analyst would ask: which option produces the greater total health gain measured in Quality-Adjusted Life Years (QALYs)? Start by listing the affected populations and estimating per-person welfare gains
Then aggregate across persons — this is the "sum-ranking" step
Next, check whether the distribution of gains matters (utilitarianism says no, only the sum matters)
Then introduce the "tyranny of the majority" worry: the 50,000 critical patients might be a minority whose severe needs are outweighed by the many minor gains of the majority
Finally, contrast this with a Rawlsian difference-principle approach which would prioritise the worst-off (the critical patients)

cards.title: The Marxist critique of liberal justice argues that liberal theories (like…
cards.subject: Political Science
cards.definition: The Marxist critique of liberal justice argues that liberal theories (like those of Rawls or Nozick) treat justice as a matter of fair procedures and formal rights within the existing capitalist framework, thereby ignoring the structural exploitation inherent in the capitalist mode of production where surplus value is extracted from the labour of the working class by the owners of the means of production. For Marx, justice is not about distributing goods fairly within a class-divided society but about abolishing the class relations that make such exploitation possible.

cards.title: Distributive justice concerns the fair allocation of society's benefits…
cards.subject: Political Science
cards.definition: Distributive justice concerns the fair allocation of society's benefits (resources, opportunities, wealth) and burdens (taxes, duties) among individuals, guided by principles like equality, need, or merit. Retributive justice concerns the fair and proportionate punishment of wrongdoing, based on the principle that offenders deserve sanctions commensurate with the harm they caused. Both are distinct dimensions of justice: the former addresses initial or ongoing distribution of social goods, the latter addresses responsive correction of norm violations.

cards.title: Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP) are non-justiciable guidelines…
cards.subject: Political Science
cards.definition: Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP) are non-justiciable guidelines enshrined in Part IV (Articles 36–51) of the Indian Constitution that direct the State to promote social, economic, and political justice by securing a social order in which justice informs all institutions of national life (Article 38) and by striving to minimise inequalities in income, status, facilities, and opportunities (Article 38(2)).

cards.title: Amartya Sen's Capabilities Approach defines justice as the expansion of…
cards.subject: Political Science
cards.definition: Amartya Sen's Capabilities Approach defines justice as the expansion of people's substantive freedoms (capabilities) to achieve valuable functionings (beings and doings), rather than merely distributing resources (Rawls) or maximizing utility (Utilitarianism). It evaluates justice by asking whether individuals have the real freedom to convert resources into capabilities given their personal, social, and environmental conversion factors.

Then introduce Sen: justice requires equal capability to be well-nourished, not equal rupees

cards.title: Social justice for marginalised groups in India refers to the constitutional…
cards.subject: Political Science
cards.definition: Social justice for marginalised groups in India refers to the constitutional and policy framework (Articles 15, 16, 46, 330, 332, 340) that provides compensatory measures—such as reservations in legislatures, public employment, and education—to Scheduled Castes (SCs), Scheduled Tribes (STs), Other Backward Classes (OBCs), and religious/linguistic minorities to redress historical discrimination and ensure substantive equality of opportunity.

cards.title: A right is a justified claim or entitlement that is recognised by society as…
cards.subject: Political Science
cards.definition: A right is a justified claim or entitlement that is recognised by society as necessary for a life of dignity and self-respect, and which is enforced by the state through legal and constitutional mechanisms; it differs from a mere desire because it represents a collective moral consensus about the conditions required for human well-being and development.
